The approach is particularly applicable to control problems involving stochastic processes defined by stochastic partial differential equations with noisy inputs, which cannot be directly solved due to the inherent randomness, but can be approximately solved using a discretized version of the Spatio-Temporal approximation method, widely employed for deterministic control problems. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated through numerical experiments on a variant of the Merton model, an financial model used for pricing options, particularly with the presence of stochastic volatility, but faces challenges due to the complex nature of its variables. The results show that the algorithm produces accurate solutions, even in scenarios with large data sets, and the Monte-Carlo estimates confirm the theoretical findings. The code developed as part of this research is openly available for reproduction. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation into quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical support. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We also outline potential observational paths for future experiments to further illuminate this field. Despite significant sensitivity, even the most advanced current detectors do not hold the necessary sensitivity required to detect the predicted anisotropy levels of sources like Active Galactic Nuclei below 10 EeV. Next-generation detectors, however, should be capable of detecting the predicted anisotropy signatures of such sources. We expect that future discoveries will be significantly influenced by the design choices of these new detectors, particularly in their sensitivity and spherical coverage. Building on the knowledge gained from our study, we propose that highly sensitive detectors with wide-spherical coverage are essential for the optimal study of extremely energetic cosmic phenomena. Furthermore, we highlight that the design of such detectors will be significantly impacted by the anticipated performance of multi-electrode detectors with cross-oriented components, which have the capability to simultaneously measure both anisotropy components and the orientation of the cosmic rays. As a result of this understanding, we suggest that future detectors with such capabilities will be best served as multi-electrode, wide-spherical detectors that incorporate multiple cross-oriented components in each unit area. Building on this understanding, we also propose that future detectors should be designed such that the signal from each of these components is treated as an individual detection event, as this approach will provide the necessary sensitivity and accuracy to fully uncover the complex anisotropy patterns of extremely energetic cosmic rays. Furthermore, implementing this design choice will also allow for the detection of quasi-spherical components, and will significantly enhance the detector's sensitivity to the study of such complex phenomena. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for the standard spheres and the unit hyperspheres in $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. The issue of wave packet spreading has been addressed by calculating the variances $A_{ab}$ as quantities characterizing the spacetime. These calculations demonstrated the typical spreading behavior typical for usual quantum mechanics. A new basis has been proposed to describe the coordinate operators $\hat x_a$ with deformed momentum operators $\hat p_a$ appearing as first order differential operators. This has enabled a straightforward definition of deformed Hamiltonian operators $\hat H$ as their closed form. The proposed approach allows speculation that the proposed operators $\hat p_a$ might be applicable as prequantization conditions. A new mathematical issue has emerged from these studies – the problem of determining the spectral characteristics of the deformed Hamiltonian operators $\hat H$ defined by their definite values of Casimir operators from the underlying Lie algebras. A simple example has been provided by solving a Schrödinger equation with a deformed position operator $\hat x$ for its ground state wavefunction within the framework of $su(2)$ algebra. The provided solutions can be viewed as new standard wavefunctions for the harmonic oscillator with a noncommutative deformation. The provided approach can be extended to deal with rotational motion and its deformed versions. The issue of prequantization can be expanded to consider the frequency parameter $\omega$ as another crucial aspect of physical systems' deformed dynamics. The provided approach can be utilized to examine the impact of quantum noncommutativity on physical systems' behavior by comparing their spectral densities

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. By leveraging contributions from multiple institutions, FL can create robust models without compromising performance, thus addressing one of the primary challenges in this field. Our approach is also cost-effective, reducing the requirement for expensive and time-consuming experiments to validate models at each participating institution. Furthermore, FL enables the development of real-world solutions for the classification of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, such as predicting patient outcomes and providing personalized treatment options. Our approach is transparent in terms of data retention, as FL models are trained locally on participant devices without the necessity for transferring training data. This characteristic is critical for engaging participants in the learning process and mitigating concerns related to data privacy. Overall, our research demonstrates the efficacy of federated learning in producing high-performance models for the classification of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, addressing one of the key difficulties in cancer research. As a result, this approach can be applied to a broad range of histopathological challenges, including the detection of cancer subtypes, polarization, and metastasis. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenxulab/FL-FISH. For additional information, please see our full paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06847. As noted in our paper, our method can be applied to various deep learning frameworks, including TensorFlow and PyTorch. Furthermore, our research is ongoing, with a focus on the efficient aggregation of data within FL, particularly in scenarios involving diverse participant datasets. Additionally, we are exploring the use of FL in real-world applications, such as collaborating with pathologists and cancer researchers at several institutions, as well as identifying potential participants through social media and online forums. As mentioned in our paper, FL has several advantages over traditional learning approaches, including improved data security and a more robust representation of diverse populations. In this research, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes three signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to high amplitude burst errors resulting from backscattered signals and underwater cable imperfections. To mitigate this issue, a modified dfé was developed by inserting an inverse frequency-dependent phase shift in the FFE arm, thereby rotating the probe signal by 180 degrees to counteract the errors. With the modified system, a maximum 2.9dB power gain was achieved, and the FFE's overall performance was optimized with a 3-tap configuration featuring a 180-degree phase shift, reducing BER by 2.5 orders of magnitude in all null regions. This research demonstrated the potential of enhanced underwater communication system performance through optimized dfé design. Additionally, the potential of the modified dfé to address limitations in fiber-optic communications was also illustrated, as the high-amplitude burst-error propagation issue encountered in this submarine cable could pose a challenge in future high-speed fiber-optic communications systems. The need for further research was also highlighted to validate the results obtained, as well as the potential of the modified dfé in fiber-optic communications. The results obtained with the modified dfé were found to be comparable to those achieved with other error correction techniques, such as maximum-likelihood sequence estimation, but with the benefit of lower computational complexity. The potential of dfé in the transmission of advanced modulation formats, such as 72Gbit/s PDM-16QAM, was also demonstrated, although the distance over which this increased data rate could be achieved was limited to 10.3km due to the restrictions of the underwater cable used in this research. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our approach, referred to as Pruning In Time (PIT), serves as a general framework that can be integrated with popular TCN architectures such as TCNs, Graph Convolutional Networks and TCN-based transformer variants. We've incorporated PIT into TPCoN, a TCN architecture that outperforms existing baselines in multiple time-series forecasting tasks. TPCoN's source code is available at https://github.com/hjdwang/TPCoN. Our method's effectiveness is illustrated through comprehensive experiments on six public datasets for time-series forecasting. Dilation factors learned through our algorithm outperform those obtained via exhaustive search in both efficiency and accuracy. Collective results demonstrate the efficacy of PIT in discovering a diverse range of optimized TCN architectures with superior performance. We've also incorporated PIT into the training process for deep learning architectures, integrating it with various optimization algorithms. Furthermore, we've conducted a detailed complexity analysis of TCNs with PIT-learned dilation factors, as well as a discussion on potential connections to previous research. We've open-sourced the code for our model, available at https://github.com/hjdwang/TPCoN. Collective experiments on six datasets showcase the efficacy of our algorithm in discovering a diverse range of optimized TCN architectures with superior performance. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. We have serendipitously identified a massive arc-like structure, dubbed a Giant Arc, which lies at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 billion light-years, this feature exhibits remarkable symmetry when viewed from space. It was discovered through a novel approach using intervening magnesium-absorbing systems in the light from background quasars. Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 30% margin of error. The Giant Arc represents one of the largest and most intriguing examples of a massive cosmic structure that could challenge the cosmological principle underpinning our current understanding of the universe. It may be an early stage in the formation of a massive structure, such as the Sloan Great Wall, which would have emerged around halfway through the universe's age. Further study of the Giant Arc will contribute to a broader examination of the universe's large-scale structure, which could provide insights into the interplay between structure formation and the properties of the universe's dark matter and dark energy components. Building on our discovery, future research will investigate the relationship between the Giant Arc and nearby massive absorbers, as well as its surrounding environment, which includes two quasar pairs that could be linked by a filamentary structure. Additionally, our team will analyze the metallicities of the intervening systems within the Giant Arc to gain a deeper understanding of its composition and how it compares to the universe as a whole. This, in turn, will allow us to use the Giant Arc as a cosmic lens to study the galaxy population at its core, which could provide a more representative sample of galaxies during the universe's middle age. This, in turn, will enable us to retrieve valuable information about the galaxy's mass-to-light ratio, dark matter content, and other key properties. This will also give us a better understanding of how galaxies in the universe's middle age assemble their mass and follow the empirical relations seen in the present-day universe. This research will be a key contribution to the study of the Giant Arc, which is a massive structure that could have implications for our understanding of the universe's middle age and the formation of galaxies. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Additionally, we developed new reduction techniques that take into account the effects of detector non-linearity and noise to calculate the aerosol depth. Through extensive simulations and analysis of real data from the FRAM telescope, we demonstrated the capabilities of this technique and the necessary calibration to ensure accurate results. Furthermore, we discussed potential sources of bias and systematic errors as well as potential avenues for further research. Additionally, we explored the possibility of utilizing this technique to derive additional properties of the atmosphere, such as dust scattering properties and optical spectral types. Finally, we discussed the potential of this technique to be utilized on a larger scale with the Cherenkov Telescope Array. This technique has the potential to contribute significantly to the development of global networks monitoring the atmosphere and could also be paired with other techniques, such as radio star link, to increase precision and confidence in measurements. This in turn could lead to a more accurate derivation of water vapor content across the atmosphere, ultimately benefiting fields such as climate and meteorology. This research was conducted as part of the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Cherenkov Telescope Array collaborations.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available online at https://github.com/ouyanghuihui/DeepHMap++. Furthermore, our model has been integrated into the Open-Pose-Tracking framework available at https://github.com/ouyanghuihui/Open-Pose-Tracking. Additionally, a model pre-trained on the ModelNet40 dataset can be downloaded from https://www.dropbox.com/s/3q5z9o3t5z1ionr/model.zip?dl=0. This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology. Despite being more expensive and difficult to work with, the Stycast lens may offer advantages in medical imaging technology. Ultimately, the use of the Stycast lens could contribute to developing low-cost, high-resolution photoacoustic tomography systems. Furthermore, the higher curing temperature of the Stycast material may offer a way to incorporate temperature-sensitive contrast agents in PA imaging. The potential of the Stycast lens also extends to other imaging technologies that rely on acoustic detection technology.

To train this model, we utilize real-world camera equipment to produce a comprehensive dataset that encompasses a wide range of blurring and illumination conditions, as well as various types of noise. By leveraging raw images and their corresponding enhanced versions in a pair-wise manner, we establish a dataset called the Blurred-Mosaicked-Noisy (BBN) dataset, which serves as the foundation for our state-of-the-art raw image deblurring and demosaicking model, Outage-UNet. Compared to existing methods and a cutting-edge demosaicking approach followed by a conventional deblurring process, our model consistently yields higher PSNR scores across all blur types and mosaic patterns evaluated on the BBN dataset. Moreover, our model demonstrates superior performance on real-world raw images featuring complex blur and mosaic patterns, recovering these images more accurately than previously possible. Furthermore, we highlight the benefits of using raw images over low-light camera images with inherent pixel repetition, which is reflected in the enhanced qualitative and quantitative performance achieved by our model. By utilizing a raw image dataset featuring multiple camera models and illumination conditions, our model also demonstrates adaptability across various input image characteristics. This is further confirmed by our analysis of the learned U-Nets components in each image processing pathway, which highlights the distinctive pattern of super-pixel repetition in raw images, resulting in the most effective demosaicking approach to date. Overall, our research furnishes a pioneering solution for the complex problem of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on raw images, which holds significant implications for low-light camera image enhancement. We anticipate this to stimulate further exploration into the unique characteristics and processing demands of raw images, which will contribute to a broader understanding of signal repetition in such images. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. Furthermore, we derive the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra from the 
Hamiltonian of the Dirac equation, leading to the identification of the $R$-Poincar\'e 
algebra generators with the total four-momentum. Lastly, we discuss the implications of 
quantizing the gravitational field within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime. 

In the context of the de Sitter spacetime, we solve the Dirac equation by formulating the 
Dirac operator as a sum of its mass term and the total four-momentum operator, which 
is derived from the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra generators. We then propose a solution for the 
wave function of a particle obeying the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime, 
which is analogous to the solution presented by Daoud and Daoud for the Schr\"{o}dinger 
equation defined within the de Sitter spacetime. We also discuss the relationship 
between the frequency of the particle and its mass, as well as the radius of the de Sitter 
spacetime, which supports the concept of Riemann spacetime. 

We conclude by highlighting the potential applications of this research in the 
development of novel materials with negative static electric resistance and in the study 
of superfluidity within cosmic string tops. Additionally, we suggest that this new 
approach may facilitate a deeper understanding of the relationship between gravity and the 
quantization of physical parameters. Furthermore, we propose that this framework can 
be expanded to include fractal and Sorkine spacetimes, which could provide valuable 
insights into the behavior of particles within these complex geometries. 

We conclude by expressing my gratitude to my research collaborators, Dr. S. Daoud and 
Dr. M. S. Daoud, for their invaluable contributions and support

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The FPG algorithm we presented can be viewed as a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. The theoretical model describing these phenomena has been verified through numerical simulations reflecting real-world experimental conditions. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method achieves comparable or better performance on actual entity extraction tasks compared to specialized techniques. We also introduce the Nested Entity Schema (NES) to standardize nested entity representations and the Nested Entity Structure Corpus (NESCor) to reflect the holistic structure of nested entities in NLP corpora, enhancing both theoretical and practical understanding. Our research and proposed methods are available at https://github.com/linusliao/NES. Our findings evidence the superiority of holistic modeling over linear modeling for nested NER, and our new benchmarks and models will propel the field forward. One significant challenge in NLP is the CoNVERge problem, which we define as the conversion of a sequence into a different explicit form. This concept is applied to develop a novel approach to sentence similarity, called CoNVERging for Similarity, which involves converting sentences into their underlying structural representations and calculating similarity based on these integrated structures. This new perspective on similarity uncovers its fundamental connection to the CoNVERge problem and is supported by substantial empirical evidence. Our proposed solution achieves notable gains in multiple similarity metrics over existing state-of-the-art models. Moreover, our work paves the way for a deeper theoretical understanding of the structure of NLP models and the inherent connections between various tasks and the CoNVERge problem. Lastly, we introduce the CoNVERge Corpus (C4) to standardize the assessment of convertibility in NLP, which complements existing benchmarks focused on other aspects. This marks the first formalization and formal NLP research challenge on the conversion of sequences. This study further explores the potential of low-rank representations in NLP, particularly in relation to the CoNVERge problem

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. I discuss two approaches: one where descriptions are created collaboratively between humans and the image description system, and another where the focus is on evaluating systems' overall performance rather than individual descriptions. Ultimately, I contend that even high-quality reference data may not fully capture the diversity of potential descriptions, which includes considerations like description length, which current ranking methods fail to account for. Consequently, I propose using description-specific metrics, such as diversity measures, to incorporate features beyond just similarity similarity. Additionally, I discuss different types of human reference data that could be utilized, including descriptions generated through various methods, such as unstructured descriptions, structured tags, and narratives, which could provide insight into distinct aspects of image understanding. Furthermore, I explore using multiple reference data sets to enhance a system's robustness and its performance when operating in real-world environments, which involve frequent updates and adjustments. Finally, I outline several research directions related to utilizing human reference data for evaluating image description systems. In conclusion, I believe that even with high-quality reference data, more consideration should be given to other crucial factors such as the system's ability to handle different descriptions, its potential for improvement, and its performance in real-world settings. Moreover, I contend that there are numerous avenues for further exploration in this domain. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Our results reveal the significance of The Big Sort in the spread of online misinformation, suggest optimizing local fact-checking efforts for areas with low social cohesion, and propose strategies for enhancing the effectiveness of antidotage campaigns by considering regional personality traits and cultural characteristics. We also found associated correlations between local phenomena and upvotes for news articles on Reddit, user engagement with comments, and differences in user demographics across regions. Finally, we highlighted the value of integrating geographical information to improve the measurement of successful fact-checking efforts and the spread of misinformation. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. These issues stem from the limited availability of high-quality resources such as semantic parsers and ontologies that can provide a rich understanding of the language used by users. As a result, developers resort to workarounds like leveraging domain-specific knowledge and using the system's own responses to define test cases. Unfortunately, this approach introduces test dependencies, rendering tests less reliable and less flexible. Furthermore, the absence of a unified representation of user utterances complicates the process of comparing test predictions with actual system responses. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach that leverages abstract action networks, a concise and unambiguous representation of desired system behavior. This framework also enables a new testing technique that can compare the meaning of utterances without relying on parsing or ontologies. As a result, tests become more reliable, flexible, and easily updateable. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a popular dialog management system. Our research offers a new direction for creating high-quality conversational systems by emphasizing the critical importance of rigorous testing. This is further underscored by the challenging experience of refining the dialog management system through testing, which highlighted the intricacies involved in crafting systems with multiple capabilities. Despite these difficulties, our testing framework proved capable of overcoming them, indicating that it has significant potential for broad applicability. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and cost-effective analysis. Several approaches have been explored for MRI QC, mostly single-factorial methods. We, however, investigated a novel strategy, encompassing three elements: subject-specific, site-specific, and scan-specific factors, to guide the classification of poor-quality MRI scans. We assembled a comprehensive dataset comprising 164,414 whole-brain 3D T1-weighted MRI scans from 33 subjects, acquired across 21 sites, with approximately 0.5% of scans classified as poor quality. Our model, pre-trained on a vast dataset, was then fine-tuned for QC tasks. We employed self-supervised learning techniques and introduced the use of scan-specific features, achieving an impressive 99.58% accuracy in classifying high-quality scans and 94.57% accuracy in identifying poor-quality scans. Notably, our approach surpassed the performance of conventional methods, highlighting the complexity of MRI QC as a multi-factorial issue. We also explored the interplay between data quality and learning, uncovering vital insights that can guide future research and developments in this domain. Our code and dataset are publicly available for the benefit of the scientific community. Furthermore, we initiated an open challenge for researchers to contribute novel methods for addressing the complex aspects of MRI QC. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae from the Pantheon sample reveals a slope of $0.61\pm 0.19$ at a 64% confidence threshold, or $0.61\pm 0.21$ at an 80% confidence threshold, indicating that the effect of cosmic acceleration on these supernovae is likely influenced by gravitational forces. Given the assumptions made and the limitations of our analysis, we estimate a minimum detection threshold of a non-zero signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 3.5:1. This result is consistent with the predictions of the Standard Model of Cosmic Physics, specifically its most well-known component, the $\Lambda$CDM model, albeit without providing new constraints on the parameters of this model. Instead, our analysis offers an alternative, more direct path to exploring the relationship between dark matter and dark energy by leveraging the relationship between gravitational lensing and the Hubble tension. Furthermore, our findings suggest that future studies using this approach may provide valuable insights into the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The techniques and strategies developed here are also applicable to larger and more comprehensive datasets that will become available through the use of upcoming surveys such as the LSST. Additionally, our study highlights the significance of using broad-band photometry in conjunction with weak lensing convergence, an effect that enhances the signal by roughly a factor of three over relying solely on photometry. This has implications for the interpretation of cosmic acceleration as a function of redshift, specifically in the early stages of the universe, a topic that will be the subject of upcoming studies. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we observed stable operation of these defect centers in a photonic environment by implementing a ring resonator design and observing no decline in spin lifetimes after switching between optical excitation and laser writing. These breakthroughs bring us closer to developing robust and versatile defect center-based quantum technology platforms that can be designed with standard SOI photonic components. Additionally, we believe our findings will contribute to the exploration of other potential quantum applications within silicon material. In this research, we explore the properties of a novel algebraic variant of the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$, as well as its corresponding degenerate Bernoulli number. This investigation is grounded in an innovative algebraic framework for generating functions and symbolic evaluation functions, allowing us to derive $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$. A complementary approach to the recently introduced algebraic method for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ is also provided, based on the recently expanded field of partial differential equations. This research is an expansion of an earlier paper and is presented in an self-contained manner. Key results and an open question are summarized in the concluding remarks. Furthermore, a companion piece focuses on the broader implications and future directions of these results.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to specific goals, such as detecting binary stars or searching for giant planets. Moreover, as the line lists are random and diverse, this method significantly boosts the confidence in the findings of the analysis and the detected planets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of applying this technique to the extensive datasets obtained by the HARPS-N satellite. By applying the optimal line lists to the data sets of EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo, we obtain the minimal RV patterns, revealing the orbital periods of these three stars as 13.09 days, 4.18 days and 4.17 days respectively. This research provides a solution to the issue of activity noise, a significant hurdle in exoplanet hunting, and can be applied to the extensive datasets obtained by the HARPS-N satellite. This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a flexible and efficient data collection process in Wireless Sensor Networks, ensuring high reliability and performance. Firstly, a link quality estimation technique is utilized, enabling swift computation of link quality between nodes. Secondly, a hierarchical sector-based system is established to organize and coordinate nodes within each sector to minimize interference and improve data transmission. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated through a protocol, called HBCP, developed and evaluated in a simulated environment utilizing TinyOS and TelosB devices. The outcome of the evaluation revealed that HBCP can achieve very high reliability levels, particularly in large-scale networks and networks prone to bottlenecks. The performance benefits of HBCP include significantly reduced packet loss, increased average throughput, and improved energy efficiency, especially in large-scale and complex networks. For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. As a result, a new benchmark named COCO-Context is introduced for evaluating object detectors that consider context. This new benchmark includes challenging evaluation protocols to assess the ability of object detectors to consider context. The protocols introduced are: considering context when there are significant background changes, considering context when there are significant foreground object changes, considering context when there are significant background and foreground object changes, and considering context in real-world applications. The results of testing the introduced protocols show that detecting objects in real-world applications is more difficult than in simulated applications. Utilizing this approach, we successfully obtained the associated momentum transformation, which preserves the four-dimensional relationship between momentum and space, p_{\mu} x^{\mu}. Following first quantization, we utilize the Klein-Gordon equation to show that Fock's spacetime corresponds to the de Sitter universe, whose spacetime radius can be defined by the invariant length representing the de Sitter hypersurface.  We also examine the implications of this approach for the massless particle, finding that Fock's spacetime leads to a plane wave solution, consistent with traditional quantum field theory.  However, a non-zero mass particle yields a bound on the energy-momentum relationship, which can be expressed as an inequality rather than an equality.  This result may be seen as an indication of mass muckiness near the Planck energy, which could provide insight into issues surrounding the stability of the Higgs field within the Standard Model.  Lastly, we explore the connection between Fock's spacetime and the Higgs field itself in the closing section of this paper.  We examine whether the Higgs field, which introduces variability into the speed of charge, may itself be responsible for the distortion of special relativity, thereby relating this behavior to the de Sitter spacetime.  If our understanding is correct, humanity has discovered a universe that varies as a charge varies, a finding that could, in the words of Dirac, 'lead to very interesting and perhaps even useful results'. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We developed an optimal acceptance policy for end-stage renal disease patients willing to accept incompatible kidney transplants. The policy, based on Q-learning, encourages patients to accept incompatible transplants if the expected benefit outweighs the increased risk of rejection. A simulation model demonstrates that the optimal policy results in a higher quality of life and a greater chance of long-term transplant survival compared to conventional strategies. The proposed approach can be applied to other complex medical decisions involving uncertain outcomes. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the exploration of the relationship between a sentence's syntax and its semantics is investigated through the case study of categorical semantics for topicography, an augmented version of the classic topicography with the added capability for sentence-level structural inferences. This extension of topicography is designed such that the topicography construction, initially a derivational operation, is now a computational flow that is both efficient and scalable, due to the use of monadic transformations to combine the effects of structural rules and the application of modalities. This resulting system is called tropico. By incorporating the control provided by the added modalities in the type system's interpretation, our approach has the benefit of avoiding the introduction of extra types or type constructors in the type system, thus preserving the calculus' infinitary, yet compositional nature. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the successful application of the proposed approach to the interpretation of the Lambek Calculus with unary modalities for the case of binary and n-ary connectives, which are redefined as controlled fusion operators. This strategy for the interpretation of structural rules and modalities paves the way for a deeper exploration of the connection between syntax and semantics through the category theoretical types and the added spin density matrix space. This connection is further examined through the study of a category theoretical semantics for the intuitionistic version of the Lambek Calculus with unary modalities and the tropico system. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research's outcomes are further illustrated through an ablation study and a broader examination of its broader impact across various multiagent learning contexts. Leveraging the learned expertise and adapting it for use in offline analysis represents valuable future research directions. This work's code is available at: https://github.com/MarcosKoeller/Rationalizable-Equilibria-under-Bandit-Feedback. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is a persistent feature, even in thick LaNiO$_3$ layers, unlike previous findings which suggested it vanished above a critical layer intensity. Additionally, our research reveals that the NMR signal's intensity is directly proportional to the slow-recovering component's amplitude, indicating that this quantity represents the carrier density. Notably, both the recovery time and carrier density display similar reductions as the temperature is increased, in accordance with the findings of other LaNiO$_3$-based research. Furthermore, our data illustrate that the spin diffusion study's outcome is unaffected by the LaAlO$_3$ layer thickness, indicating that the interface resistance between LaNiO$_3$ and LaAlO$_3$ layers is negligible. Lastly, our research discovers a straightforward relationship between the spin diffusion time and the square of the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, with a constant diffusion constant unaffected by temperature. This relationship can be described by the expression $T_1^{-1}(t) \propto t^2/(1+t/L)^2$, where $t$ represents the time and $L$ the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness. This discovery provides a more precise understanding of the LaNiO$_3$ layer's spin dynamics, potentially shedding light on the underlying causes of the slow-recovering component. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the correlated metallic state of the LaNiO$_3$ layer is unaffected by the LaAlO$_3$ layer's thickness, offering implications for the design of devices utilizing LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices. This knowledge may also be applicable to other interface-coupled systems, such as strained metals on substrates with different properties. Ultimately, this research underscores the value of $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR as a tool for investigating the electronic properties of systems like LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. By utilizing the model, the researchers discovered that the response of the jet flame to acoustic vibrations in the high-frequency range is similar to that observed in lean mixtures, while it is affected by heat loss in the low-frequency range, which actually increases reaction rates rather than decreasing them as previously believed. The findings from the study address the limitations of previous studies on the subject matter while also providing a framework for investigating the dynamics of jet flames within other applications. Additionally, it highlights potential research paths for a broader range of topics, such as the interaction between jet flames and their surroundings, the effects of flow turbulence on reaction rates, and the response of these flames to acoustic vibrations in different scaling regimes. A linear approach was successfully applied to a massive methane-air jet flame by both its inner core and outer layers, while producing results that align with those obtained from LES simulations. The outcomes from the study also revealed that very large-scale structures play a significant role in determining reaction rates in a way that is unaffected by the type of turbulence model used, whereas further analysis is required to fully comprehend the role of intermediate-scale structures. Furthermore, the research demonstrated that both inner and outer layers of a jet flame respond differently to acoustic vibrations in different frequency ranges, while also showing that heat released from the flame's fluctuations in response to acoustic vibrations is not enough to extinguish the flame

We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional flows in general,
focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our predictions align with numerical simulations.
The findings reveal that our new expressions for shock heating rates provide a
more accurate account of the internal shock dynamics.
The solution also highlights the significant difference in wave energy preservation
at large radii between head and tail shocks, with a potential greater impact on
matter ejection. This distinction emphasizes the importance of waveforms in
shock evolution.
We also predict shock behavior to transition from weak to strong and utilize
this to estimate mass loss in scenarios involving rapid sound pulses and minor
central explosions. Furthermore, we discuss the possibility of this phenomenon
leading to the generation of relativistic shocks and the associated high-energy
emissions. Additionally, we explore the possibility of this wave-driven shock
being responsible for the gradual decline often seen in explosions from massive
stars. Simulation results show that even relatively weak transients can lead to
extensive matter loss, albeit microlensed. On the other hand, steeper transient
light curves can result in greater matter loss, potentially exceeding $\sim
10\rm{M_\odot}$. Analysis of available data does not rule out this phenomenon,
and it is suggested that this potential wave-driven shock could be a common
feature in stellar outbursts. Lastly, we discuss how this mechanism could
potentially lead to the conversion of gravitational energy into directional
blastwaves in massive stars experiencing outbursts that do not result in collapses
or direct expansions. This could also imply a more prolific occurrence of fast
transients in the early universe, driven by massive stars experiencing outbursts,
followed by rapid sound pulses. This could, in turn, lead to additional detection
of fast transients in the early universe with upcoming more sensitive telescopes. 
Also included are three supplementary documents.
One discusses the basis for approximating the conservation of adiabatic invariants,
the origin of which dates back to the work of Chandrasekhar in the 1940s and '50s.
The other two documents address potential difficulties related to shock behavior
and wave-driven explosions

geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity for multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This 
connection bridges Diamond--Sasaki's findings to earlier generalisations of 
Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects. 
Notably, we exploit and develop innovative techniques using geometric 
modularity, specifically Serre--Tanke's framework, in addition to new insights 
into Galois actions on weights, to arrive at our conclusions. 
Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for potential applications of our 
methods to more intricate cases. 
Notably, we provide a preliminary analysis of potentially geometric $G$-covers, 
which may be of independent interest. 
This involves new restrictions on the monodromy of $L$-functions and their 
derivatives, which may also be of interest in the broader context of potential 
non-algebraic weights geometric modularity. 
As a result, we are able to establish links between geometric and classical 
approaches to modularity, leveraging and expanding on earlier research of 
Diamond--Sasaki, Bruggen--Ginsberg--Sasaki, Holmes, and Pimentel. 
This, in turn, enables us to expand on earlier generalisations of Serre's conjecture, 
specifically focusing on weight aspects, which may also be of independent 
interest. 
We also develop and exploit new insights into Galois actions on weights, which 
may also be of independent interest. 
We provide a detailed analysis, including all necessary details on potentially 
geometric $G$-covers, all of which is an innovation over our initial 
announcement.

weights" on the research forum 'Homotopy Theory and Algebraic Geometry' at

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This research develops an algorithm capable of identifying the minimum number of nodes to split (among them, specific target nodes belonging to distinct groups) and a particular splitting of those nodes, given that the resulting graph depiction has no edge crossings and specific layout constraints are met. A key aspect of this algorithm is its limited dependence on instances, as its running time and memory usage are bounded by a quantity directly related to the number of nodes to be split, not their actual values. Though the algorithm itself doesn't provide the optimal solution, its ability to be optimized further makes it a good starting point. Furthermore, this research includes an efficient approach to identify edge crossings by developing a new grouping of nodes (between distinct groups) and assigning corresponding split node pairs, followed by a more efficient method to determine if a specified node can be moved to a different group, thus allowing the consideration of more complex node relationships. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The ability to learn from incremental datasets, even those that change over time, remains a key issue. Incremental learning algorithms can tackle this problem by adapting to new classes and retreating from outdated ones, a process known as inc-INC or inc-DEC, respectively. A novel inc-DEC algorithm based on a deep neural network is introduced in this paper, called Inc-DecNet. This innovative approach involves calibrating the network's output distribution to counteract the problem of drifting decision boundaries and alleviate the impact of new classes on previous ones. Inc-DecNet's performance is compared to other state-of-the-art inc-DEC algorithms through a comprehensive evaluation of 7 benchmark datasets, resulting in superior or on-par performance compared to the baseline methods across all evaluated datasets. Furthermore, Inc-DecNet's advantages over other approaches are highlighted by a detailed error analysis. This paper also introduces a comprehensive survey covering inc-INC and inc-DEC algorithms, a summary of inc-DEC's applications, and a thorough error analysis of inc-INC and inc-DEC. Finally, potential future directions for the field are also discussed. This research is an initial step towards developing inc-DEC algorithms using deep exotic networks, such as self-dual networks, and Inc-DecNet is publicly available on GitHub under the MIT License. Its code has been integrated into the Open-Source Inc-LEARL Repository on GitHub. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between sensing and computing tasks. Computing tasks, although demanding, can be executed by any agent, while sensing tasks require specific agents with unique capabilities and can be performed efficiently. We introduce a framework where self-interested agents make decisions based on payoffs and analyze the equilibrium strategies resulting from their individual self-interested actions. We demonstrate that in a robust system where connections between agents are unpredictable, the most efficient computation can always be achieved through a form of coordination. Additionally, we explore how providing agents with preference preferences or metagame information can both positively and negatively impact the effectiveness of the system, potentially even leading to suboptimal outcomes. We validate our theoretical findings through both analytical and simulation-based approaches. This research contributes insights relevant to the design of distributed robotic systems. We start by classifying these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Lastly, if the M\"obius curvature R is negative, we demonstrate that the compact hypersurface undergoes a process of singularities in a finite period of time. Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific medical imaging technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. Furthermore, there is a shortage of high-quality, specially tailored data sets for training models on rare conditions such as TOF.

For this research, we first evaluated how accurate models become when they are trained with publicly available, labeled data sets (specifically, the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC) set) and then tested against CMR data obtained from TOF patients, without any prior use of such data during training. Following this, we sought to identify which additional information, either on the data quality or the underlying medical imagery, or a combination of both, is more beneficial for further improving the results.

We experimented with two different approaches to training these neural networks: first, training them on high-quality CMR data sets alone, and second, training them on both high-quality and lower-quality CMR data sets. In the case of the former method, the challenge lies in the limited amount of high-quality data available for training. In the case of the latter method, the issue becomes the limited amount of labeled data available for guidance.

In comparison to challenge leaders, our top-performing models exhibited 5.8% and 4.4% greater average Dice coefficients when evaluated against an independent, externally-sourced TOF data set following both training and testing protocols identical to those employed during evaluation for the MICCAI 2020 AutoDose Challenge. Moreover, our research demonstrated that incorporating guidance from segmented images, as opposed to raw image data, yields substantially better results. Additionally, using a larger, more comprehensive data set consisting of diverse CMR images proved to be highly beneficial with an average reduction of 5.6% in segmentation error rate. Lastly, we found that extracting and incorporating additional information from the images, such as heart borders and regions, rather than just using raw image data, yields substantial gains with an average reduction of 11.8% in segmentation error rate. This research may also offer valuable insights to those working on other medical imaging segmentation tasks

Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Code is available at https://github.com/youfu12/towards-general-object-detection. This research further paves the way for enhancing the robustness of object detection in real-world applications. Additionally, a new, scale-aware evaluation metric called IOU-based Scope (IOS) is introduced to measure the scale generalizability of object detectors. Its soundness and reliability are verified by qualitative and quantitative analyses. Furthermore, a new, scale-specific IOS metric is proposed to quantify the scale performance of object detectors. This new evaluation framework complements the existing mean average precision (mAP) metric and is applicable to various object recognition tasks. Its code is available at https://github.com/youfu12/ios-evaluation-metric. This work's advancements are expected to contribute positively to the development of robust object detection in real-world scenarios. Nevertheless, several open issues in object detection remain unresolved and could serve as intriguing research challenges for future studies.
