Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. This groundbreaking research offers an alternative and unbiased approach to estimating the distances to galaxies across the universe. Furthermore, as the detection capabilities of powerful astronomical instruments improve in sensitivity, a vast amount of new data on planetary nebulae frequency distributions will become available, enabling this groundbreaking method to accurately measure the distances to galaxies on a larger scale in the future. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We introduce a novel, adaptive framework capable of implicitly identifying optimal loss functions for each sample, thus outperforming both specialized loss functions and the baseline choices. Our results demonstrate a regularized outcome when employing different loss functions, highlighting the potential for further advancements in deep learning through the exploration of alternative loss functions. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. By employing a specific Lyapunov function and a energy-based approach, the stability of the closed-loop system is demonstrated. Furthermore, the controller's effectiveness is verified through numerical experimentation. Building upon previous research, this study expands the applicability of boundary feedback stabilization to account for oblique orientations between the direction of the control and the boundary where the input is applied. This development is particularly significant in optimizing the design of boundary feedback controllers. Leveraging the established framework, the study's findings on stabilizable boundary feedback controllers are shown to be directly applicable to other fluid dynamics equations, such as the Boussinesq equation and rotating Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, the study's approach to achieving stability is illustrated through a simplified boundary layer problem, demonstrating the relevance of its results to these broader applications. Notably, this study's findings on the Navier-Stokes equations are validated through numerical simulations, with all necessary proofs and details on the approach's applicability and the derived bounds on the gain operator already being addressed in a companion paper.

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. To our knowledge, this is the first time a learning algorithm has been tested in a real-world robotic setting using a range of noisy feedback types. Our code is available at https://github.com/vayalee/learning-from-fake-feedback. This study delves into the implications of these discoveries for the formation of colliding black-hole - neutron-star binaries, including a notable candidate such as GW190426_152155 reported in the second Gravitational Wave Catalogue. Furthermore, it examines the influence of birth velocities and neutron star sizes on the generation of such systems, along with any potential electromagnetic counterparts associated with them. In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using a mixture of Rb-87 atoms, where the existence of this coupling was shown through the dissemination of a superposed state and the rotation of an atomic pseudospin. We further illustrated its applications by constructing a two-body entanglement and an inter-orbital coupling-based phase gate. Notably, these results occur in an unscaled, universal unit of measurement, allowing for straightforward comparison with theoretical predictions. Additionally, our study uncovered an novel phenomenon in which the inter-orbital coupling coefficient may be modulated through light shifts, presenting new opportunities for controlling coupled states. Furthermore, the characteristics of this coupling were found to be robust against misaligned laser beams, a potential issue in similar experiments. Finally, we outline potential pathways for observing the effects of this inter-orbital coupling first-hand, specifically in one-dimensional systems, where the occurrence of this coupling can lead to the creation of Majorana fermions. This inter-orbital coupling may also be adapted for use in quantum simulation of various models, such as the Hofstadter model and the Bose-Hubbard model, with the possibility of universal application due to its scalable and controllable nature. This includes the simulation of one-dimensional systems with periodic boundary conditions, despite being demonstrated in an expansive, two-dimensional setup. Furthermore, our study indicates that this inter-orbital coupling may be a universal feature, potentially present in systems involving more than two orbital states. This understanding may be generalized across various species, potentially expanding the scope of applicable systems. This research offers a novel, precise, and scalable approach for generating inter-orbital coupling, a crucial element in the development of robust and scalable quantum technologies. This includes the creation of universal quantum gates, as well as the simulation of complex phenomena, such as superfluidity and Bose-Einstein condensates, making it an important breakthrough in the field of quantum physics. This study provides a detailed, step-by-step explanation for generating inter-orbital coupling in atomic systems, featuring a freely available, customizable, and easy-to-use code for implementing this research, available at https://github.com/USP-QuAntUS/Implementation-of-inter-orbital-coupling. This code allows users to execute the necessary experiments to observe inter-orbital coupling in practice. Furthermore, this research is part of an ongoing project to develop a robust and scalable proof-of-concept for quantum simulation, encompassing a suite of codes available at https://github.com/USP-Qu

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space. The algorithm is subsequently expanded to accommodate the generation of a specific class of polyhedra in $d$-dimensional hyperbolic space. A newly created polyhedron in three-dimensional hyperbolic space is also presented. The underlying mathematical theory, namely the combinatorial approach to polyhedra, is also briefly reviewed. Additionally, the adopted notation and terminology are defined in the appendix. A previously overlooked polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space, here referred to as the 'double-hexahedral 3-pyramid', is incidentally identified through the application of the algorithm. It is characterized by having a Schutte graph identical to that of the truncated 3-cube, yet its face vector differs from the latter. The name 'double-hexahedral 3-pyramid' is proposed for this previously unreported polyhedron. It is demonstrated that the double-hexahedral 3-pyramid, cannot be obtained through the gradual extension of the trivial polyhedra. It is also shown that it is a member of a broader class of polyhedra derived from the extension of the trivial polyhedra in a combinatorial manner. It is then proven that this new class of extended polyhedra is transitive. Its fundamental properties, such as its Schutte graph, face vector, and orientation vector, are presented. It is also proven that all polyhedra in three-dimensional Euclidean space can be obtained through the application of the Eisenlohr-Farris algorithm. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the double-hexahedral 3-pyramid is an intrinsically regular polyhedron. It is also shown that its vertex coordinates can be determined through the application of its symmetry operator. It is then proven that all intrinsically regular polyhedra in three-dimensional Euclidean space can be obtained through the application of the Eisenlohr-Farris algorithm. It is also demonstrated that the double-hexahedral 3-pyramid is an orbit of the 3-dimer. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Finally, we've established connections between unclonable encryption and other cryptographic objectives, including non-invasive attack on quantum protocols and creating various forms of quantumly-secure multiparty protocols from unclonable encryption schemes. Our results demonstrate the value of exploring unclonable encryption in the quantum realm. Our research is an evolution of the authors' previous work presented at TCC 2020. We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles of MoS_2 layers, potentially aligning them with
excitation spectra of NMs like quantum dots or carbon nanotubes. Furthermore,
plasmon-phonon hybrid modes were identified and we demonstrated the scope for
controlling flat plasmons via electromagnetic fields. Our research provides a
theoretical framework for understanding flat plasmons in 2D materials with flat
bands and suggests they could facilitate novel applications with twisted
bi-layers. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of combining theory with
experiment to map TDMT/AA MoS_2 systems through inter-band plasmon absorption. When
MoS_2 layers are stacked in a TDMT configuration, plasmon absorption appears at a
longer wavelength than in the AA stacked form, and this shift is shown to be
angle-dependent. A model describing this phenomenon also indicates a link to
superconductivity in some twisted bilayer graphenes. Overall, our research
highlights the promise of flat plasmons in 2D materials with unusual electronic
structures and suggests they could facilitate novel applications with twisted
bi-layers. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of controlling flat
plasmons via electromagnetic fields and a sophisticated theoretical description of
these systems. While our research focuses on MoS_2, we anticipate similar
plasmononic behavior in other transition metal dichalcogenides. Consequently, we
believe our findings are relevant to the broader class of 2D materials with
unnatural electronic spectra and our model is applicable to a wide range of TMDs.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It highlights the potential for further research and
insight gain from treating stars and planets as analogous objects in the study of
their magnetic atmospheres and wind flows. It also emphasizes the value in
systematically exploring similarities and differences between these two kinds of
celestial bodies. High-energy radiation from wind interactions can impact a planet's
ability to sustain life, making a deeper understanding of the magnetic field's role
critical. This review concludes by highlighting potential paths for further
theoretical and observational research in this field. It also discusses the need
for more sophisticated modeling that takes into account the intricate processes
affecting both stars and planets, as well as the requirement for a unified framework
that can explore these processes across both types of celestial bodies. This review
is an expansion of the author's recent talk presented at the 18th Pacific Asia
Journalists and Scientists Conference. The author would like to express gratitude
to the organizers and the host institution, as well as to colleagues and students
who contributed to the research and facilitated the discussion. The author would
also like to extend appreciation to the editor and the referee for their helpful
feedback. The author would like to acknowledge the support received from the

Fellowship (FL180100112) and the ARC's Centre of Excellence for Astrophysical

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies rather than hierarchical processing
of sentences for the Basque task, and our subsequent modifications to the
models yield improvements indicative of the ability of sequential models to
learn about the language's grammatical structure.
The improvements are, however, only observable when the models are trained
on both the question and the answer sets, suggesting that such training
is a prerequisite for the neural networks to grasp the language's structure.
The findings provide valuable insights into the capacity of sequential models
to comprehend the underlying structure of language and the potential of Basque
as a test bed for studying the succession of linguistic elements within a
sentence. The study's results may not be exclusive to Basque and the proposed
methodology can be applied to the examination of other complex agreement
phenomena in languages. The models' performance on the agreement prediction
tasks can be observed at https://github.com/andersonbrito/linguistics/tree/master/basque_agreement. HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may also provide insights into the planet's mass and atmospheric properties. Furthermore, accurate transit predictions may enable researchers to detect secondary eclipses more easily and potentially identify other planets within the HD80606b system. The new ephemeris and data on the planet's orbital path are available for use by researchers and telescope networks around the world. These findings also highlight the effectiveness of collaborative telescope networks, such as the Global Telescope Network, which can provide high-quality data on complex celestial events while minimizing costs and risks associated with using a single large telescope. The data and the approach described in this study may also be of value to scientists who aim to utilize transit and eclipse events in the light curves of exoplanets as natural probes, such as searching for the presence of stars or the detection of exoplanet magnetic fields. The recently released schedule for JWST observations of HD80606b, which include a critical study of the planet's atmosphere during a transit and a close approach to its host star, has been ensured to be efficient and aligned with the updated ephemeris. The schedule takes advantage of the fact that the closest approach to the star, known as the periastron, occurs in late 2022 and will not happen again until six years later. The new data and the updated ephemeris will be submitted to the Transiting Exo Earth Survey, Telescope Data Archive

Our focus is on developing an isogeometric analysis capability for these models, tailoring the existence of weak solutions and the convergence of the discrete scheme, and ultimately leveraging these results to inform the development of an isogeometric phase-field model for fracture in such structures. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, as a broader investigation, we examine the feasibility of these searches across a range of processes involving the exchange of bosons, considering both the direct detection of these particles and their influence on the decay products, known as leptons. While the discovery of vector leptoquarks would provide clear evidence for new physics, we must also consider other explanations for potential anomalies in experimental data. To this end, we explore additional mechanisms involving vector leptoquarks that could mediate the observed breakdown of lepton-flavour universality. While these scenarios could contribute to the detected anomalies, we also note that they could result in the production of additional particles, such as taus or certain heavy mesons, in excess of the standard model predictions. The code developed in this study is now an essential component of three beyond-standard-model search codes recently submitted to the CERN Open Data Initiative, which provide detailed simulations of event signatures in experiments involving the collision of protons at the LHC. Furthermore, as experiments at the LHC continue to analyze increasingly complex processes and event signatures, the level of theoretical precision in predictions and simulations will need to be raised to take full advantage of the available data. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, deep learning's reliance on vast datasets for training makes it vulnerable to data-driven attacks, such as training models on tailored artificial data, which hampers the practical application of such methods. Furthermore, deep learning models are ineffective at incorporating physical constraints, such as the consistency of quantum mechanics, which form the basis for accurate PET reconstruction algorithms, such as maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). This research introduces a novel uncertainty-aware deep learning framework that combines PET and MRI data for enhanced image quality, while incorporating physical constraints and quantifying uncertainty to prevent overfitting and output distortion. The proposed framework's performance was verified with in-simulation and real-world data, demonstrating its capacity to create high-quality PET images from low-dose PET data and accompanying MRI scans, outperforming state-of-the-art deep learning models and traditional PET reconstruction methods. The results indicate that the proposed framework achieves comparable performance with only a tenth of the required training data, offering a more practical solution for clinical settings. The framework's code is available online at the provided repository link. The findings suggest that low-dose PET imaging, without the use of chemical agents like MRI dyes, can be performed safely and efficiently in pregnant women and young individuals by combining physics-based PET reconstruction with deep learning and robustness to out-of-distribution data, potentially expanding the applications of PET imaging in these populations. The proposed framework's performance with real-world data, particularly from a specific study on pregnant women, is also presented and shows its effectiveness in reducing PET doses, but further research is needed to fully explore its potential in these sensitive groups. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within a text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. The study's findings are verified using multiple computer systems that recognize connections within a text and a wider range of texts on various topics. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Notably, our approach yields an explicit description of an upward spanning forest if the graph is upward planar. We've also introduced a parameterized version of the Upward Spanning Tree problem, which can be solved in polynomial time with respect to the graph's treedepth parameter. We've further investigated the parameterized complexity of several variants of the Upward Planarity problem, including a version where edges are assigned weights and the task is to determine whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout using edges from a given set. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Finally, our findings also demonstrate how quantum information theory can be integrated with the Lie-hauler vector approach, facilitating a deeper understanding of operator growth and entanglement within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems. Overall, this combined use of quantum information theory and group theory provides a more comprehensive framework for studying operator growth and entanglement in Lie-symmetric systems. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among the approaches evaluated, including the utilization of conventional methods. The results showed that the proposed hybrid approach using the MAUS-ML model yielded the most accurate estimations, outperforming conventional methods. The innovative hybrid approach described also provided insights on enhancing the accuracy of geospatial distance estimation. To this end, a new objective function for optimal feature selection was introduced, along with a technique for ensemble modeling. The proposed algorithm was then applied to enhance the accuracy of geospatial distance estimation between WiFi fingerprints, leading to the development of the optimal hybrid solution, called Multi-Feature-Optimal Hybrid Solution. The results obtained with this approach demonstrated a significant reduction in the mean squared error, from 8.21 to 5.37, and a mean absolute percentage error of 59.16%, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art techniques. The novel approach described, along with the proposed algorithm, provides a framework for the optimal selection of machine learning algorithms, suitable for a wide range of applications in the field of indoor localization. The algorithm's versatility, as demonstrated, makes it ideal for utilization in various real-world scenarios involving the location of individuals or devices within indoor environments. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. The research also reveals that in multi-pass energy recovery linacs, beam breakup usually becomes more unstable in later passes, although the exact behavior depends on various factors, including pass details and energy gain per pass. To confirm the validity of the model, the derived threshold current for a specific energy recovery linac design matches experimental data from the Fermilab Me-PAc/ADET demo straight section. The study includes detailed beam-RF system parameters for the demo project and highlights the importance of carefully considering filling patterns during the design of multi-pass energy recovery linacs to optimize performance. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth. In the case of 1 M solar systems that form planets within 1 million years, we discover that water soaked particles lead to rocky planets, while particles with high sticking forces result in giant planets composed of refractory materials, and particles with super-dry sticking forces lead to cores of planets that are unstable and will be consumed by the surrounding disk, although this could be avoided in systems that form planets in a shorter time frame. In the case of smaller systems that form planets in a shorter time frame, we discover that water soaked particles lead to planets with substantial crusts, while particles with high sticking forces result in planets with metal-rich cores, and particles with super-dry sticking forces lead to planets with magma oceans. In the case of 0.01 M solar systems that form planets in a shorter time frame, we discover that water soaked particles lead to planets with extensive mantles, while particles with high sticking forces result in planets with large cores of refractory materials, and particles with super-dry sticking forces lead to planets with extensive silicate atmospheres. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our research provides a comprehensive solution for nonlinear hard constraints in imitation learning, potentially far-reaching implications for its integration with other planning methods. Additionally, EKMP's flexibility makes it a suitable candidate for complex robotic tasks, such as the assembly of Cori, a challenging puzzle piece. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ethz-assistive-robotics/ekmp. Furthermore, we introduce the Hard Constraint Imitation Learning (HCIL) benchmark suite, a comprehensive set of obstacle avoidance tasks suitable for evaluation and further advancement of future nonlinear hard constraint imitation learning algorithms. Our research shows that kernelized movement primitives can achieve high performance on linear constraints, but may not fully utilize their potential on nonlinear constraints. Our work also addresses the issue of normalization in kernelized movement primitives, and we introduce a normalized version of these primitives. Our research provides a detailed analysis of EKMP's constraints, its application to complex robotic tasks, and a comprehensive evaluation of its performance. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by calculating their distance to R, excluding pinning based on trivial equal distance to R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest elements is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the distance between vertices is capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some properties of beta_k are examined along with its behavior under expansion of a graph to its largest component. A method is presented for calculating beta_1 in a graph more efficiently than regular distance calculation. It's also shown that certain types of vertices can be added to a graph once-dimensionally independent of its original properties. Finally some conjectures are made and disproven as a way of exploring the properties of beta_k. Typically beta_k increases linearly with k but sometimes remains constant at k=1, at k=2 or at some number greater than 2. Three distinct sub-classes are defined for graphs with a constant beta_k equal to 1, 2 or another number greater than 2. A graph with a particular property has a specific name when its beta_k is 1. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. A key advantage of this method is that it can be executed using just a subset of available data with no need for extensive processing resources. Furthermore, this study lays the groundwork for applying machine learning to other high-energy astronomy data sets, such as those from the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor and upcoming instruments like the Arcus and Amoeba all-sky monitors. These monitors, capable of detecting even brief outbursts across the sky, will profit from machine learning's ability to efficiently analyze a vast amount of data covering the entire sky. In contrast to traditional methods, this study's machine learning approach uses the unique characteristics of its training data to define a suitable image processing filter, one that effectively detects and analyzes complex astronomical sources, patterns, and phenomena. This method facilitates low-latency detection of transient and variable sources, as well as accurate analysis of global and multi-component phenomena, like giant flares and bursts from distant binary systems. Additionally, this algorithm can be used to create custom maps emphasizing specific sources or phenomena, like searches for extraterrestrial intelligence or massive astrophysical events, by training the model on relevant features and then applying it to the full data set. This technique's flexibility allows for deep learning-based expansion of the feature space, a capability that sets it apart from more conventional machine learning approaches. In comparison to traditional Fermi-LAT data analysis methods, this algorithm delivers superior results, particularly for complex, multi-component spectra, and roots out hidden sources and structures in just a few seconds, a fraction of the time required by existing methods. These improvements, combined with reduced memory usage and processing times, result in a significant reduction in costs, both in terms of human expertise and infrastructure. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. This metric assesses the degree to which the achieved social welfare surpasses the highest possible social welfare that could be achieved by any serial dictatorship action sequence. We find that certain of our proposed solutions display a high price of serial dictatorship indicating scope for further improvement of their performance. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical framework with clear practical applications for designing efficient and effective solutions to a broad class of optimization challenges. We hope this study will contribute to an expansion of the scope of problems that can be addressed via optimization of serial dictatorships, as well as the development of new and better algorithms for solving these types of problems. We have made our research available under an open-access arrangement that facilitates both review and replication of our results. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. Ultimately, our analysis at optimal Pan-STARRS1 conditions yielded 
three new wide binary prospects alongside one confirmed binary asteroid, 
ALECA-001, whose orbital separation fits binary stability models. Additionally, 
our research revealed various asteroids exhibiting marked deviations from average 
single asteroid profiles, potentially featuring additional wide or tight binary
configurations. Among these potential binaries, ALECA-002 through ALECA-007, 
ALECA-009, and ALECA-010 exhibit deviations indicative of binary or irregular
shapes, while ALECA-008 presents a profile suggestive of a triune or tight 
binary or irregular target. Furthermore, our wide field surveys' analytical 
approaches outperform the results obtained by ALECA, a narrow field survey 
specifically designed to detect binary asteroids. Consequently, we propose 
utilizing wide field surveys' analytical approaches on available archival data. 
Such analysis on available archival data from the Palomar Automated Telescope 
and PIRATE narrow field surveys yields one documented wide binary asteroid, 
while that of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's analytical approach discloses one 
additional wide binary asteroid, Elnodea. As a result, the total number of 
documented wide binary asteroids within this diameter range now stands at 11.  This research was conducted with funding from the NSF Graduate Research

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal Bayesian detector, and develop a simplified approach for optimizing a related detection method, before supporting our findings with numerical simulations. We also consider potential applications of spatial modulation and multiuser detection in scenarios such as device sensing and image decoding, and provide examples of these use cases. Further, we investigate ways to optimize the parameters of the system and its components, such as the number of transmit antennas, and demonstrate the effectiveness of these optimizations through numerical simulations across a variety of scenarios.  This research provides a comprehensive analysis of spatial modulation and multiuser detection, including examples of its practical applications, and shows the efficacy of these techniques across a range of use cases and system configurations.  We hope this work will contribute to the development of advanced communication systems and the exploration of new techniques for spatial modulation and multiuser detection. We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, diagnostic diagrams, and
multi-wavelength images. Leveraging client-side computing advantages, these tools
offer complex analyses and calculations, including diagram computations, such as
BPT, N2, and mass-radius estimations using luminosity and surface brightness relations.
Furthermore, our approach enables rapid development of custom visualization components
to address novel astronomical data visualization needs. By open-sourcing these tools,
we aim to contribute to the astronomical community's web development initiatives and
foster collaboration and code sharing in this area. The code for these visualizers
is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/astro-rcsed/rcsed-frontend, under
the permissive MIT License. We invite collaborators to suggest features and improvements.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma. learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images.  The
code and models are publicly available on https://github.com/Chen6758/BIML.  The

proposed framework offers an appealing solution to the long-standing challenge
of medical image segmentation.  The key advantages of our framework are its
robust performance with limited annotated data, the ability to handle complex
images, and the versatility in accommodating diverse medical image
segmentation applications.  One potential direction for further research

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the feasibility of training an AI to manage the complexities of multi-agent, scenario-based interactions, which may also be applicable to broader conversational settings beyond role-playing games. Our challenge and methodologies are openly available at https://github.com/aleksivas/G4C, inviting others to explore the possibilities of conversational guidance through the D&D framework. Our study has been included as an extended abstract in the proceedings available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04403. New developments in the field have also been described in another submission at this conference, Building on Learned Dungeon Master Strategies with Human Players, which can be accessed through https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07144. These advancements showcase the potential of our approach, as evidenced by the improvement of performance metrics observed in further experiments reported in https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07144, which primarily focus on the D4R4 challenge that we introduced and described in this paper. Additionally, we have explored the application of our G4C framework to the game of Star Trek: The Next Generation, which is detailed in the extended version available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04403. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. They can be extracted from experimental data via Boer-Mulders function-like interpretations. Our model predicts relationships between these new functions and their counterparts in the Sivers and Collins functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that one of these new functions has a direct connection to the spin alignment of partons in the infinite momentum frame. If they are found to be nonzero, they would indicate that parton spin alignment is not solely caused by the movement of individual quarks, but also by quark-quark correlations within the proton probed by different virtual gluons. This would mark a significant shift in our understanding of hadron structure. Our proposed new functions provide a framework for explaining the positive results obtained in experiments at COMPASS and RHIC, which showed that quark and gluon polarization are not proportional to the square of the charge, as predicted by the perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Instead, our new functions offer a more intricate view of parton behavior, influenced by quark-quark correlations within the proton probed by virtual gluons, which also supports the idea of extending the parton distribution function to a quark-quark correlation distribution function. This concept can be applied to other hadrons, such as neutrons, protons, and mesons, which could provide valuable insights into the universal nature of parton distribution functions. Our work also raises questions about the underlying nonperturbative quark-quark correlations within hadrons, which could be explored through our proposed new functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This research demonstrates how geometric and topological analysis can guide the understanding of protein folding and its complex phenomena like knottiness. The methods developed here can also be applied to the study of other complex phenomena in biology and chemistry. Additionally, the data analyzed in this study is now available as a reference set for the community, providing valuable insights that can be utilized in future studies. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Additionally, we explored variations of the EDE model, including an early dark energy model with a varying equation of state parameter $w$, with results showing that its nature could be investigated using upcoming galaxy surveys like Euclid. Furthermore, our research also delves into the implications of dark matter neutrinos and finds that existing limits on neutrino masses actually increase slightly, with existing data constraining the product of neutrino mass and sterile neutrino temperature ratio to $0.12^{+0.20}_{-0.07}$ ($68\%$ C.L.). Existing data already provide significant constraints on the EDE model, with improvements in data leading to even tighter constraints on its parameters. These constraints will be useful in analyzing upcoming galaxy surveys like Euclid, which are expected to significantly narrow down the range of the EDE parameter $f_\mathrm{EDE}$. Euclid is expected to determine the EDE parameter with a precision of $0.020$ ($68\%$ C.L.), which is in line with the findings of a related study. Additionally, our research also explores the combination of EDE with other cosmological components, including an early dark energy component with a varying equation of state parameter $w$, with results showing that existing data constrain its nature to be consistent with a constant $w$ equal to $-1$, with a slight margin of error. Existing data actually place a limit on the equation of state parameter $w$ at $-1.07^{+0.21}_{-0.08}$ ($68\%$ C.L.). With such tight constraints on the EDE model, its properties will be accurately determined using upcoming galaxy surveys like Euclid, which will significantly narrow down the range of the EDE parameter $f_\mathrm{EDE}$.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional NG theorem. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed, enabling the computation of quasi-Heisenberg algebras in a systematic manner. Through effective field theories, the implications of these algebras were shown to result in physical consequences, such as massive spin-zero Nambu-Goldstone bosons, spinning NG bosons, and flavor symmetry breaking. A central hypothesis proposes that the anomalous NG theorem can be understood through the geometric approach of Cartan algebras and manifolds. With this context, an explanation for the quasi-Heisenberg algebra has been provided, drawing from mathematical concepts of noncompact simple Lie algebras and manifolds. A striking connection between the anomalous NG theorem and the universal Hopf algebra has been established. Building upon these foundations, an even more general framework has been posited as the Universal Anomalous Theorem. A framework for Lie symmetries has been identified as the Anomalous Noether's Theorem. Furthermore, our research has led to the creation of the Quasi-Heisenberg Algebra Database, a comprehensive repository of quasi-Heisenberg algebras derived from Lie symmetries across various fields and theoretical frameworks. This database serves as a valuable resource for physicists and mathematicians to explore the intricate relationships between Lie symmetries, geometric structures, and fundamental theories. A hypothesis has been proposed that the application of advanced mathematical technologies to the study of Lie symmetries could yield novel insights into the universal principles governing nature. Finally, our research has resulted in the development of several educational courses and seminars on the anomalous NG theorem, quasi-Heisenberg algebras, Lie symmetries, geometric structures, and number theory, with the aim of disseminating this knowledge to a broader audience. These educational initiatives have evolved into the creation of various theoretical databases and have provided the foundation for several ongoing and future research projects in our group. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The DISCO framework's effectiveness is further validated across three diverse NLP tasks in our research. The code and counterfactual data produced using the DISCO framework are publicly accessible at https://github.com/google-research/disco. This research is a part of the Stanford AI Funded Project, and we present our findings at the DISCO workshop @ ICLR 2023. Wordings in several languages have been translated from the original title "DISCO: The Development of Counterfactual Studies at Stanford" for reference purposes. Additionally, we have made the counterfactual data available for the Sentiment Contrastive Learning Benchmark (SCLB) at https://github.com/google-research/disco/tree/main/sclb. This research has been funded by the Stanford AIFP and the outcomes have been presented at the DISCO workshop @ ICLR 2023. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This research may also offer a solution to overcoming high-cost substrate issues during high-pressure gas reaction processes. The technique involves using a graphene blanket to coat the interior surfaces of reaction chambers, allowing the easy recovery of clean substrates for further use in epitaxial processes. This approach is particularly useful for the synthesis of ultra-clean Heusler compounds when using high-reactive elements such as boron. This processing technique allows for the easy preparation of clean graphene surfaces, removing the difficulty of incorporating volatile boron elements into Heusler compounds through the remote epitaxial process. This has the added benefit of preventing the contamination of reaction chambers with difficult-to-remove amounts of oxygen and moisture. This approach to remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene has significant potential to broaden the range of materials that can be grown on graphene with greater precision and quality than existing methods. This includes the successful growth of the topological insulator Heusler compound GdBiTe. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  Furthermore, this new approach extends the potential for adapting existing single-positive datasets to promote the development of novel techniques in the field. The code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/SP2ML. This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligns with the original energy at time zero and as time approaches infinity. The upper bound can be perceived as a nonlocal-in-time modified energy, which includes both the original energy and a cumulative component stemming from the memory effect of the time-fractional derivative. Specifically, it demonstrates that the original energy actually declines as time passes in a localized area near the starting point. Although the theory mainly focuses on the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, it can be applied to other time-fractional phase-field models like the Cahn-Hilliard equation.

This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. We also introduce a broader algebraic framework that encompasses non-commutative algebras, for which the GNS construction still yields an algebra-unitary state relationship. This relationship is expressed through an adjoint connection that reflects the algebra's underlying monoid structure. This more comprehensive framework can be seen as forming part of a higher-categorical framework that encompasses directed graphs and topological algebras. We further establish that the GNS construction can be viewed as part of a co-variation, a fundamental mathematical structure that captures the relationship between physical states and observables. This co-variation provides the basis for recovering the algebra's structure from its associated state, a process that is shown to be linked to the algebra's ability to support unitary representations. However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation. The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices. The technique's effectiveness is validated through extensive simulations and practical applications. The proposed method also offers a practical solution for integrating cardiac diagnosis systems into overall healthcare systems. The technique's potential for application in medical diagnostics is a significant area of research with wide-ranging implications. The paper's research findings provide a clear insight into the development of cardiac diagnosis technology. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The framework's efficacy is verified through three notable experiments: a self-collected dataset for wearable activity recognition, the Physionet57 dataset for strong transfer learning, and a real-world experiment in collaboration with Apple Watch users. Overall, FedHealth offers a pioneering solution for addressing the practical challenges of machine learning in wearable healthcare. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in efficient learning for temporal sequences. Compared to conventional techniques, incorporating simultaneous supervised learning and metric adaptation enhances prediction accuracy in both synthetic and real-life scenarios, according to our results. Furthermore, the features identified by relevance learning show impressive comparisons to those of alternative methods. Additionally, our method allows for the visualization of low-dimensional grid data, highlighting the temporal structure in the data. This visualization facilitates the interpretation of results and reveals the learned temporal patterns. In conjunction with the identification of variable importance, our results demonstrate the capacity of our system to extract valuable information from temporal sequences. This is accomplished through the application of delayed relevance learning. In the context of our experiments, involving the classification of microbial communities and the prediction of HIV drug therapy, our system demonstrates the benefits of delayed learning over traditional approaches. This is reflected in the improved performance of our system, as evidenced by lower error rates and scores in relevant metrics. In the case of the HIV therapy prediction task, our system achieved exceptional performance, with an accuracy of over 90%. This was accompanied by the feature importance map, indicating the dimensions considered most relevant by our system. These dimensions corresponded to those with established significance in the progression of AIDS. In contrast, our method may struggle with sequences comprising highly correlated variables. To address this limitation, we introduced a technique called Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time with Variable Blocking, capable of handling such datasets by dividing the variable set into independent subsets. This enabled our system to efficiently learn for temporal sequences in complex life science measurements. This was demonstrated through our experiments with gene expression profiles from multiple cell types, as our system successfully learned from the temporal sequences in each dataset. Additionally, we explored the capability of our system to handle datasets with missing values, as well as the integration of prior knowledge into the learning process. This was successfully achieved through the application of imputation techniques and the incorporation of prior knowledge into the relevance learning

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance. To that end, we
first establish upper and lower bounds for the problem, and then we provide a
generalized formula for the sequence reconstruction problem, as well as its variant. 
Finally, we discuss some specific cases for the sequence reconstruction problem. 
It's worth noting that all the provided codes and the majority of the problem
solutions can be found in the associated supplementary materials. Last but not

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy.
