Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. Notably, we discovered that while models excel in answering questions focused on individual claims, they consistently underperform in cases that require integrating information from multiple claims. We anticipate future work to incorporate additional datasets that cover a broader range of sources, which, along with the proposed QASPER dataset, will serve as a foundation for advancing the field of Question Answering over complex documents. Our initial experiments highlighted the difficulties faced by current models and revealed several intriguing findings, including the observation that human responses often summarize key information from multiple paper sections, the discovery of a significant performance gap between models that excel in other Question Answering tasks but struggle with these challenges, and the identification of question types that either easily integrate information from the paper title and abstract or instead require a more thorough document reading. Furthermore, our proposed Span-Based Model, which leverages a combination of a cross-checker and a document encoder, represents a pioneering attempt to address this challenging Question Answering task, but it still lags behind human performance, especially when evaluating models that integrate additional information from the paper body. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Finally, it contemplates the potential of artificial systems to surpass the limitations imposed by natural materials' inherent symmetry constraints. High-quality experimental data, particularly in photonic systems, are expected to play a pivotal role in further developing our understanding of topological nodal lines. Last, the review concludes by highlighting the promise of artificial systems in exploring novel, uncommonly accessible regimes of parameter space that could harbor topological phenomena. Nonetheless, achieving a true, long-wavelength topological nodal line line remains a significant challenge. A more feasible approach might be to design structures that create nodal lines within a limited momentum range or around exceptional points rather than in the extended zone center. A deeper theoretical understanding of these phenomena is crucial and further breakthroughs are likely to stem from a symbiotic interplay between cutting-edge experiments and advanced simulations. In conclusion, artificial systems have demonstrated an ability to replicate complex topological phenomena observed in natural materials, encompassing points and lines of nodal crossings, and we anticipate that future advancements in this field will provide valuable insights and new opportunities to explore the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Deeper analysis of MAG-Net's performance reveals the association between radiologists' annotations and model predictions, and network visualization shows the diverse nature of tumors in distinct views.  The organization and complexity of tumor tissue, as identified by radiologists, are also reflected in model predictions and are dependent on the view used.  Consequently, using all three views with MAG-Net yields better results than using a single view or just coronal and axial views.  Furthermore, compared to radiologists, MAG-Net's performance varies depending on tumor type but consistently falls short in certain instances.  Overall, this research demonstrates the potential of deep learning-based solutions to detect and diagnose brain tumors but also highlights the importance of clinical collaboration and careful consideration of challenges associated with real-world applications. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our results demonstrate substantial improvements in the quality of recovered textures and illumination compared to baselines and existing differentiable renderers, particularly in the face of noisy and limited training data. Our pose and deformation reconstruction approach also achieves accurate results, even in scenarios with minimal training, primarily due to the accurate shadow rendering, which is then shared with the optimization of geometric parameters. Our approach and experiments evidence the superiority of sophisticated yet efficient and differentiable shadow computation over simpler yet less accurate alternatives. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Our research provides a data-driven framework for developing fast and adaptable models that can handle dynamic riverbed profiles, transforming the prediction of river flow velocities into a continuous process. The proposed models also exhibit potential applications beyond river flow velocity predictions, where the incorporation of probabilistic geostatistical variables can enhance the performance of deep learning algorithms in data-driven applications. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Moreover, surprising benefits are observed as EOWS also enhances model generalizability and improves performance on unspecified tasks despite training, without requiring additional fiscal costs. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. It's also demonstrated that this strengthened condition applies broadly, serving as a key tool in our subsequent proof of Tamar Zieglers' conjecture. 

Furthermore, we explore potential applications of this rule to sets of larger size (greater than three times the size of four), even if the associated sumset isn't as optimal, which could provide insights into the broader Freiman theorem. 
In addition to this, we develop an alternative, more flexible approach to Freiman's 3k-4 theorem, which could be paired with other theorems to yield novel results and might also be of interest on its own.

This leads to the classification model overfitting to the easy cases and results in limited improvement in reducing false positives after proposing accurate relationships. To address this issue, we created a parallel branch in the pipeline that uses a classifier to identify proposed relationships and eliminates easily incorrect ones before passing them to the classification model. This reduces the number of relationships entering the classification model by 70.7% while maintaining overall accuracy. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. This is further supported by the fact that the galaxies in this group exhibit a 2:2 rotational pattern and shared minor-axis, indicating collaboration during their formation, ultimately forming a pair of interacting galaxies. This is also shown through the detection of ultrabright z=2.91 Ly$\alpha$ and C$\rm IV$ systems, indicative of a highly accreting black hole in the group's core. This is further discussed in a companion paper.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Analysis of incoming solar proton flux did not meet the required threshold for this process in previous events from 2000 and 2003, in contrast to the much higher proton flux recorded on November 7, 2004. A second day's worth of data from the Bolivia detector revealed a continuing but decreasing solar neutron decay proton flux, below the background level by the evening. This event and the one in 1989 have the highest recorded proton fluxes linked to solar neutron decay, the lowest detection thresholds and the most precise time frames of the three known instances, making them particularly significant in the study of this process. A second, smaller solar flare from January 6th, 2002, detected by the Bolivia detector, may also be associated with solar neutron decay. Furthermore, in the search for additional instances of this process, a new, more sensitive technique for identifying its signature has been developed, with the goal of utilizing recorded data from numerous, previously under-exploited solar proton detectors around the world. This new method, more precise and accurate than previous approaches, combines the characteristics of several solar flares that produce solar neutron decay, their associated proton fluxes and characteristic time frames, allowing for a more in-depth understanding of this process and the potential it holds for generating false positives in searches for antimatter, such as that undertaken by the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer on board the International Space Station. This information, combined with recorded data from solar proton detectors, may provide insight into a long-standing cosmological question regarding the abundance of antimatter in the universe. In addition, in the search for this process's signature, the development of new, more sensitive detectors and detectors with improved detection thresholds, such as those for the Bolivia and Mexico locations, as well as the re-examination of data from various solar proton detectors around the world, may also yield additional, valuable scientific payoffs in the search

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. We cover various techniques for grasping neural networks, including local explainability, visual analysis, and debugging. Moreover, this study delves into various methods for global understanding, such as network optimization, as well as both quantitative and qualitative performance metrics. We also discuss various tools and techniques for both local and global understanding. Finally, we discuss and demonstrate the applicability of these methods to spinal cord damage detection using magnetic resonance images. Although considerable progress has been made in the field of DNNs, significant challenges persist, including issues related to low-quality training, overfitting, and the influence of robust optimization methods on network behavior. We anticipate that future research in the field of XAI will further illuminate the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. We hope that in-time publication will allow for the inclusion of our work as a part of this progressing body of research in the field of XAI. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events, especially when there is a lack of preliminary knowledge available. Furthermore, the fact that different sources provide varying types of information about events makes the detection even more complicated. To address this challenge, our proposed MetaFEND model builds upon the idea of neural process models by incorporating differentiating hyperparameters that enable the learning of general representations from data related to events. By doing so, the model can efficiently utilize both event-specific and general knowledge from various information sources, such as social media posts and reliable news articles. The MetaFEND's ability to learn from few examples and incorporate prior knowledge from a range of information sources is proven through experiments on the Flickr and NeutralKratos datasets, resulting in superior performance compared to existing methods. Moreover, the results demonstrate the benefits of the model's meta-learning capabilities in detecting false news from various information sources, especially when there is only a small amount of labeled data available for training. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that, unlike commonly examined isotropic and uncoupled systems, a system with an anisotropic coupling and strong spacial relationships may exhibit robust and resilient valley interference patterns and Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction.
This discovery also enables the implementation of precise placement of dopants to control the exchange interaction.
As a result of this research, the possibility of realizing novel functionalities, such as quantum valley and spin interference effects, is now feasible.
In addition, this study's insights may also be applied to other group-IV semiconductor systems, such as carbon and germanium, to explore their fundamental properties.

Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Our approach is particularly relevant to complex systems involving multiple interacting components, where graph neural networks can provide a unifying framework for exploring related topics such as the interplay between structure and behavior in adaptive networks and the implications of homogeneous vs. heterogeneous connections on various computational processes. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed and their strong quantum nonlocality proven, contributing to a better understanding of the relationship between UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality. Additionally, a condition for certain multi-qubit UPBs was established to have strong quantum nonlocality, and several near-optimal UPBs of large size were constructed and their strong quantum nonlocality proven, facilitating the exploration of this phenomenon in larger systems. Furthermore, a connection between the size of a UPB and strong quantum nonlocality was identified, and various examples of UPs that fail the established condition were shown to have strong quantum nonlocality, demonstrating that the condition is not necessary but not necessarily sufficient either. Finally, the relationship between this phenomenon and others, such as entanglement and contextuality, was also considered, contributing to a better understanding of strong quantum nonlocality in heterogeneous systems. In the conclusion, several promising research directions are presented, including the examination of this phenomenon in systems with a large number of parties, the construction of optimal UPBs, and the investigation of contextuality in UPBs.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. The algorithm's simplicity and astrobot-specific safety features prevent the generation of invalid or collision-causing trajectories, eliminating the need for check-assembly and recovery paths. This approach has been integrated into the SDSS-V's coordination system and successfully tested at the Kaneohe Bay Observatory. Experimental data analysis indicates that our method produces consistent results and can handle a wide range of target distributions, as well as unusual astrobot configurations and lost or malfunctioning devices. This comprehensive coordination framework has addressed the survey's coordination challenges, paving the way for implementing safe and efficient astrobot systems in optical multifiber spectroscopy. This work has implications for other multifiber spectroscopic surveys employing coordinate-based astrobots. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. Further, we identify a twin variant within our constructed series of graphs, which helps demonstrate the applicability of a broader theorem also proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger. That theorem serves as a key component in the proof of a more comprehensive result regarding infinite families of locaily arc-transitive graphs on finite orbits. Finally, we formulate an open question related to possible associations between the graph theoretical twisted wreath class and certain infinite families of bilinear forms. As well, we establish another infinite family of locaily arc-transitive graphs by making use of a broader framework, thereby proving a slightly more general version of the mentioned broader theorem of Giudici, Li, and Praeger. Lastly, we show that one of the new infinite families of locaily arc-transitive graphs contains a subgroup isomorphic to the symmetric group $S_3$, which in turn enables us to provide a counter-example to yet another broader theorem also proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Additionally, this approach enables the development of models that not only excel in few-shot learning but also achieve high scores on natural language questions without any further fine-tuning. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. This model has the potential to address fundamental questions regarding the impact of disease on brain circuits and circuit-based interventions. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the value of collaborative work between theoretical models and experimental data from animal Parkinson's disease research. The model has been published in a publicly accessible repository for the benefit of the computational neuroscience community. It is anticipated that this model will contribute to the advancement of brain circuit research and the development of more effective treatments for Parkinson's disease. The code for the model can be found at https://github.com/yutok ParkinsonsModel. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Our findings also suggest a link between the power of an active galactic nucleus and the outflow of gas, a relationship that is influenced by the phase of a merger. Therefore, data we collected with the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for optical galaxy mergers has significant implications in the field of astrophysics and physics of galaxy mergers. To further build on these discoveries, we propose follow-up observations with the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for (1) deeper analyses of gas flows and active supermassive black holes in galaxy mergers and (2) the collection of data on gas flows and active supermassive black holes in galaxy interactions that are not part of the GOALS survey. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. We show that our proposed interpolation function yields more accurate results than the standard linear interpolation operator, revealing the method's potential applications in numerical solutions of partial differential equations and scattered data interpolation. The new interpolation function is examined in comparison to the standard linear interpolation operator, revealing its potential advantages. The code utilized in these experiments has been made publicly available. The analysis of the new interpolation function's convergence rate is discussed, along with potential modifications to the quasi-interpolation formula. Further potential extensions of the new interpolation function are also considered. The code is written in Python 3.6 and is compatible with the PyGAM and PyGAM2 libraries. The results of the experiments are presented in the form of tables and figures. The new interpolation function is defined by the equation U(h,x,y) = (1/2)*tanh((3/2)*h^-1*(x-y)), and is derived from the hyperbolic tangent function. The quasi-interpolation formula is based on the Wu-Schaback approach, and is defined by the equation Q(f,h,x) = ∑(N*(x-i*h))*(U(h,x-i*h)*(f(x-i*h))). The convergence rate of the new interpolation function is analyzed by defining a distance metric, and is proven to converge at a rate of O(h^2) through mathematical expansion. The comparison of the new interpolation function with the standard linear interpolation operator is conducted through absolute and relative errors, and is optimized using the minimax principle. The numerical experiments presented demonstrate the superlinear convergence of the new interpolation function in certain cases, and the potential for further optimization of the interpolation results. The new interpolation function is more precise in approximating functions that increase linearly with the distance, and is derived from a transcendental interpolation function based on the hyperbolic tangent. The original quasi-interpolation formula is modified to accommodate the new interpolation function

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. These findings are crucial in preparing for the full deployment of upgraded forward pixel detectors as part of the CMS upgrade package. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an quantum tomogram of arbitrary light states. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of quantum tomography, particularly in the Wigner-Husimi phase-space tomography, facilitating their detection without the need for full state reconstruction. We also analyze the accuracy of this approach by simulating the reconstruction of two-light-state Wigner functions from their tomograms, showing that this method yields precise results. Furthermore, this approach offers the advantage of tomogram data already being measurable experimentally, making it a practical solution for detecting the mentioned phenomena in laboratory setups. Additionally, this approach can be expanded to address other problems related to the detection and analysis of quantum light states.

Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. Moreover,
we find that incorporating role constraints superiorly enhances the model's
emotional intelligence and politeness, as verified through additional human
evaluations. Ultimately, our research facilitates the construction of open-domain
dialogue systems that can meet various role specifications, enabling them to
engage in more natural and effective human conversations. To further the field,
our models, data, and implementation details are made publicly available at:

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy solely by these means can be misleading due to the influence of external factors such as weather conditions and disease stages. To address this issue, we developed a reliable method to evaluate pesticide strategies by standardizing treatment outcomes on a per-unit basis, eliminating the effects of variables beyond farmers' control. This approach reduces variability, allows for meaningful comparison of treatments, and makes interpretation of results more manageable. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through an analysis of strawberry disease management data, which revealed that early intervention with fungicides significantly reduces crop losses in moderate disease stages but may even increase losses in severe disease stages. This approach can be applied to other pest management scenarios with similar datasets, offering a valuable tool for researchers and the pest management industry. 

This research was conducted with support from the Western Center for Pest Management, a National Institute of Food and Agriculture grant, and the California Strawberry Commission's Research Fund. The data and R scripts used in the analysis are publicly available on GitHub, providing a comprehensive framework for evaluating pest management strategies. 

The case study on strawberry disease management highlights the importance of precise timing for fungicide applications, a practice that can lead to suboptimal results if carried out at the wrong stage. The optimal approach depends on standardizing treatment outcomes on a per-unit basis, accounting for factors such as disease stages. If this adjustment is not made, the perceived benefits of early intervention may actually be detrimental in severe disease stages. This finding has implications for the broader pest management industry, as it demonstrates the value of a detailed stage-based approach in evaluating pest management strategies. The method developed in this study is applicable to other pest management scenarios with similar datasets, offering a useful tool for researchers and the pest management industry.

The results showed that early intervention with fungicides significantly reduces crop losses in moderate disease stages but may even increase losses in severe disease stages. This has important implications for the optimal timing of fungicide applications. The method developed in this study is a generally applicable solution for evaluating pest management strategies.

require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Furthermore, the superior performance of the proposed
model is less dependent on training dataset size. Ultimately, incorporating
video subtitles data into the prediction process results in a more effective
and robust model. The proposed model's effectiveness is validated through
user studies in addition to prediction accuracy evaluation. The model's code is
also made available through a GitHub repository named vpp-360-video-subtitle. The
repository's code is based on PyTorch deep learning framework and can be
replicated with required data available at GitHub/360-virtual-tourism-video-sb. The model's capability is further verified by conducting additional user studies in different settings. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as periodic variations in these measurements. A problem this experiment faced was the presence of sudden, temporary anomalies known as glitches that could mask a signal from this principle. This paper calculates the statistical significance of any periodic variation found in the data and discusses the characteristics of glitches. It is shown that a specific glitch model has characteristics similar to those of other, more complex glitches and therefore using a general statistical approach to analyze the data is reasonable. This approach involves comparing the periodic variation found in the data to the minimum the test could detect in the absence of a signal. The paper also presents an updated estimate of how well the experiment could test this principle, assuming that new data from the experiment will have the same characteristics as the data analyzed in this study. It is found that in the most sensitive test, a violation of this principle that is 10% as large as the laboratory-based standard could be detected with a 95% confidence level. The specific glitch model used in this study was based on data from the Michaelson-Morley experiment and was not designed to account for variations in the gravitational field across the Earth's orbit. While this experiment was not sensitive to such variations, future tests of the weak equivalence principle under stronger gravitational fields may need a more complex glitch model that takes these variations into account. If the source of a signal from this principle cannot be confirmed by independent means, its validity will also need to be established compared to a specific benchmark of periodic variations found in the data. This modified estimate is confirmed by an explicit model, which demonstrates how the calculated variance can lead to a scale-invariant TMD gluon distribution. This distribution's momentum dependence is governed by a logarithmic function of the square of the gluon's momentum divided by the square of the regularization scale, and is independent of the choice of this scale. Furthermore, the calculated variance yields a scale-invariant dipole gluon distribution when the regularization scale is set to the intrinsic transverse scale of the incoming hadron, and this leads to a logarithmic $x$ dependence in the wave function's amplitude. This behavior is in line with lattice QCD predictions, and indicates that the wave function's logarithmic $x$ dependence may arise from the interplay between non-linear small-x saturation and IR renormalons. This implies that the predicted logarithmic $x$ dependence should be observable in upcoming experiments at the future electron-proton and proton-proton colliders. This research's findings have important ramifications for the investigation of IR renormalons in color dipole distributions, and the associated development of better perturbative approaches to describe small-x phenomena. As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Building on the method introduced in ['Frog Model on a Tree: Transience and Recurrence', arXiv: 2012.04367], we identify the precise threshold for the critical density. Specifically, the frog model is recurrent if the density exceeds the degree of the tree, and transient if it stays below this threshold. We also establish that the fundamental ratio of the frog model on a d-ary tree, when it is defined, is equal to its degree. Furthermore, we show that this critical density can be achieved in an ergodic ergodic measure, which we refer to as the'supercritical phase'. We name the measure ergodic because it behaves similarly to the stationary measure when the frog model's behavior is not influenced by the tree's structure, and'supercritical' because it occurs when the frog model's behavior is influenced by the tree's structure. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. A generalization of SGR, called the Multiple-Source Geodetic problem, is also introduced and analyzed. Chordal graphs allow for the resolution of SGR in O(|E|) time, and a generalization of this efficiency is discussed. An analysis of the impact of vertex duplication on SGR, and the associated costs, is presented, along with the description of an applicable algorithm. Further research into the properties of vertex duplication, including its effect on graph connectivity, is also discussed. A conclusion to this study is provided, along with suggestions for additional research avenues. The results and methods described can be applied to the development of geodetic indices in social networks and supply chain management. An open question regarding the complexity of SG, and several generalization of SGR, is presented, along with the derivation of an applicable algorithm for a specific instance of these problems. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Furthermore, our method's ability to adapt to different environments, detected via sunlight indicator and lighting sensitivity, ensures optimal performance and minimal pose-sensitivity issues. Moreover, the application of our method is not limited to a specific robot arm model and can be applied to other similar arm models with minor modifications. Additionally, we have explored extending our method to utilize both depth and RGB camera data for even more accurate estimations, and the augmented code is provided in the supplementary materials available on GitHub. Experimental data indicates our novel approach offers superior performance, ease of use, and user-friendly interface in comparison to existing markerless and machine-learning-based methods. With an emerging interest in collaborative robots operating in diverse environments and settings, the development of such advanced and precise extrinsic calibration systems is crucial for enhancing their overall performance. Furthermore, our model's unique design and unique solution to the problem also makes it an ideal candidate for future research in calibrating and optimizing non-rigid robots and artificial muscles. Furthermore, the introduction of our model is timely as there is an ongoing shift from traditional fiducial marker-based calibration methods due to their reliability, precision, and versatility in a variety of applications. In contrast, traditional methods have several disadvantages including the expense of the markers, the time it takes to place them, the difficulty of placing them accurately especially in tight spaces, the need for a second camera for tracking, the limitation to planar environments, the difficulty of calculating end-effector pose from keypoint data, the rotation of the end-effector, and the fact that they require extensive expert knowledge and training. In contrast to these methods, our model offers several advantages including the elimination of the cost and time associated with purchasing and placing the markers

Our findings also reveal specific characteristics of biharmonic hypersurfaces with these operators. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a biharmonic hypersurface within the Euclidean space has either the curvature or Ricci operator acting on it in a recurrent manner, it implies that the hypersurface is an open set with minimal points. Consequently, if the Ricci operator or curvature of the hypersurface is recurrent, we can determine that the biharmonic hypersurface is comprised of minimal points. Moreover, we establish that if the Jacobi, shape, or Weyl operator of the hypersurface is recurrent, the hypersurface itself is an open set with minimal points. A significant aspect of our proof involves establishing and utilizing the following theorem: if a hypersurface has a recurrent biharmonic operator, then it has a global 1-st eigenvalue in the Euclidean space. We also prove that if the hypersurface has a recurrent Jacobi or shape operator, it implies that the hypersurface is an open set with a 1-st eigenvalue. Conversely, we prove that if a hypersurface has a 1-st eigenvalue and its curvature or Ricci operator acts in a recurrent manner, it implies that the hypersurface is biharmonic. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To accomplish this, we developed a set of protocol specifications in the form of template programs using the Tamarin prover, which can be easily extended to cover other database protocols. Our findings can be useful not only for verifying the consistency guarantees of MongoDB's transaction protocols but also for developing a more general framework for the formal specification and verification of transactional protocols in distributed databases. Our work has already inspired the authors of the MongoDB documentation to update the descriptions of the database's transaction protocols based on our findings. Our research was conducted with the support of the STARS research fund provided by NUS. Our paper was initially intended as a technical report but has now been submitted to the 25th ASE conference for consideration. Our work has also been presented at the FLoC Doctoral Dissertation Award Ceremony and the NUS STARS Research Talk Series. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. 

 

Despite some variability, the overall pattern remained the same, and the slight variations in the mean energy flux values from the four approaches were largely caused by the different times at which the solar wind energy distributions were observed, which themselves varied in response to the changing cycle of solar activity. 

 

We also discovered a relationship between the flux and anisotropic components of solar wind energy, where the highest levels were found at nearly 90 degrees to the solar radius, but with some variability depending on the specific approach and the underlying conditions that shaped the solar wind. 

 

Based on these findings and the fact that the solar wind energy distributions were much more orderly and normally distributed than seen from farther out in the heliosphere, we believe that a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution may not be accurate in modeling these phenomena, and instead, research should focus on a bi-Maxwellian distribution that can account for the observed variations and the distinctive characteristics of solar wind energy flux across the solar surface. Moreover, understanding these processes is crucial for enhancing our knowledge of a variety of solar phenomena and the mechanisms that produce them, as well as the potential impacts on spacecraft and the safety of human explorers in the harsh environment of the solar surface and the heliosphere.

Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases. of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators. The proposed methodology is relevant
to other scalar-valued shortest path problems in spatial networks.  We introduce a
new measure, called super-epsilon, which characterizes the precision of discrete
shortest paths in relation to continuous optimal solutions, and we explore its use
in designing networks for optimal discrete-continuous trajectory optimization. The
study of free flight trajectory optimization leads to a new formulation of the
discrete-continuous shortest path problem as a sequence of super-epsilon-bounded
minimization problems, capturing the error in discrete solutions relative to the
continuous optimal solution. This formulation provides a framework for addressing
other error-bounded discrete-continuous shortest path problems in spatial networks.

range of wind field patterns, and we show that it results in solutions that are
optimal in theory but may not guarantee the same precision in practice due to

The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Furthermore, the complexity of these signals is found to be influenced by the velocity of the traction, rather than the force applied. This research is also accompanied by an analysis of the interrelationship between these signals and the mechanical properties of the tape, particularly its surface roughness. Overall, this study offers a significant advancement in the understanding of mechanical systems characterized by nonlinear, dynamic, and complex behavior, and its methods can be adapted to other such systems in the future. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs simultaneously. Through exhaustive experiments on widely-recognized benchmarks, our MD-CSDNetwork exhibition consistently superior performance across various evaluation metrics, thereby establishing a new performance benchmark for deepfake detection. Furthermore, the inherent adaptability of our proposed network results in enhanced robustness against accommodation-related performance degradation, a previously unaddressed concern in the field. Moreover, the comprehensive analysis of our findings, supported by qualitative and quantitative insights, provides a comprehensive framework for the comprehensive evaluation of deepfake detection algorithms. The code and pre-trained models for the proposed method are publicly available at: https://github.com/seyon-lee/MD-CSDNetwork. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. This is particularly beneficial in graph-structured networks with hierarchical levels, as our method facilitates more flexible and optimized device updates. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our analysis identifies the governing rules encoded in the smart contract's code, its energy consumption, and the environmental impacts of transaction validation. By examining the code's technical aspects, our study fills the gap in existing research on the intersection of blockchains, smart contracts, and pyramid schemes. Lastly, by looking at ten additional, recently created pyramid schemes built into blockchains, our work highlights the ease with which such schemes can be devised and the potential for great financial harm caused by them. By understanding the advantages and disadvantages of pyramid schemes built into blockchains, our study aims to contribute positively to the development of more secure and transparent blockchain-based systems. Our research is also a warning to users about the dangers of pyramid schemes, particularly those hidden within smart contracts, and the need for better protection against such deceits in the cryptocurrency world. Ultimately, our work highlights the critical importance of user caution when investing in unproven schemes and the need for more effective detection methods for deceptive smart contracts. By better understanding the code used in such schemes, we can develop more reliable contract verification tools and a more effective strategy for preventing the creation of harmful pyramid schemes. Our study also shows that the success of a pyramid scheme built into a blockchain depends heavily on the capabilities of its code and the reach of its promotional content, rather than the inherent characteristics of blockchain technology. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. With this correction, the accuracy of the velocity-based model is enhanced to the same level as the dipole-based model, making both methods equivalent in terms of precision. Furthermore, we found that both methods can be made consistent by applying a correction to the vector potential, thereby facilitating the direct integration of tight-binding models utilized for description of dark states and other phenomena into full Maxwell-Bloch simulations. This research provides the foundation for the development of tight-binding models that can be used in a wide range of applications, spanning the study of light-matter interactions in quantum architectures and the optimization of interaction times for ultrafast spectroscopies. Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Specifically, it has been found that one of these poles exhibits significant width not typically associated with its mass, implying that a broad and weak fluctuation component within the RPA framework actually results in a wide and dispersed peak upon evolution from a collective state. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that this broader resonance, designated as a quasicollective state, may also be found in other cyclable channels for excitations. A direct connection exists between the widths of both collective and quasicollective states and their respective reaction matrix elements. Furthermore, research has also demonstrated that the quasicollective state's broad width can also be explained through alternative methods that consider RPA poles in a self-energy context. A key aspect of these studies has been the utilization of a consistent RPA Hamiltonian matrix, which has been demonstrated through both direct and indirect evidence. Ultimately, the discovery of a broad resonance within $^{16}$O has significant implications for our understanding of heavy, collective state excitations across the nuclear chart. A notable implication of these findings has been the subject of some controversy, with certain researchers questioning the consistent RPA framework used in these studies. A response to these concerns has been incorporated into the revised manuscript. A new approach to resolving the controversy surrounding these results has been explored, with a solution that may be applicable across the nuclear chart. Further investigation into the nature of collective and quasicollective states has led to a breakthrough understanding of these states, which has been summarized into a key finding that such states generally adhere to a rule where the sum of their widths and residues equals a constant value derived from the reaction matrix. A demonstration of this rule has been provided through specific examples of states within $^{16}$O. A notable aspect of these state's broad width has been the identification of a universal relationship that connects the width-residue rule with the quasiparticle nature of RPA states.

By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. Additionally, we made the player location data valuations open-source available for external use.

Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique, called VisPars, uses neural networks to recognize both types of text but treats them as separate features rather than identical. By employing a binary classification system and a template-free approach, VisPars avoids the limitations of traditional holistic methods.
