We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Finally, we propose a connection between asymptotic monotone independence and the critical behavior of certain universality classes in statistical physics. This connection, however, remains purely heuristic. As such, the terminology 'universality class' is used here in a descriptive sense only.

Moreover, our work is expected to foster a broader investigation of type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, and monotone freedom in the context of random matrices and matrices associated with stationary processes. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. To verify our approach, we simulate our results across various parametric configurations and observe corresponding outcomes from our analysis and the actual multilayer Kuramoto system. Our findings are relevant to any vector-valued Kuramoto system on a multilayer network and can be used to better understand the robustness of synchronized states in complex systems. To conclude, we discuss how our method can be used to explore multilayer networks by reducing their complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In doing so, we demonstrate how our approach can be applied to other complex systems and provide a basis for further research into the dynamics of multilayer networks. Additionally, we examine how our results can be used to validate thekuramoto.org, a web-based platform for simulating and analyzing Kuramoto systems. Through our results, we demonstrate how our approach can be used to simulate and analyze complex systems and discuss how these findings can be applied to other fields of research. In the conclusion, we summarize the main contributions of this research and discuss potential avenues for further exploration. In the final section, we provide a comprehensive overview of the main concepts and key results from this research, highlighting the main achievements and outlining the main contributions. Furthermore, we discuss the main findings and provide a detailed explanation of the results, along with a discussion of the underlying principles. In the closing remarks, we reflect on the underlying principles of this research and discuss the underlying mathematics. In the appendix, we provide a detailed derivation of the reduced system for a multilayer network with an interlayer connection between two nodes. In the supplementary material, we provide a detailed explanation of the underlying mathematics used in this research, along with a discussion of the underlying principles of this research.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein's operator can be obtained from the standard wave operator in curved spacetime when using his famous field equations remains an unresolved issue in the field of differential geometry. Additionally, obtaining the standard wave operator as the compatibility operator of the wave equation in curved spacetime appears to be impossible if the curvature does not vanish. In such cases, the obtained operators behave analogously to the Einstein operator on conformally flat spacetimes. Furthermore, this work also provides a comprehensive classification of all compatible operators with the Cauchy operator, drawing a clear distinction between the types of differential modules they define - either torsion-free or with non-trivial differential rank. This distinction leads to a comprehensive identification of an operator's parameters, resulting in a significant expansion of previous findings, namely those of Gilkey and the authors of [19]. Their earlier work, although groundbreaking, was conducted under the restrictive assumption that the curvature of a manifold must be non-degenerate. In contrast, this research demonstrates that abundant new information becomes accessible when this limitation is lifted. In consequence, the extended theorem on the spectrum of the Dirichlet operator for a manifold of variable signature, previously proven in [19] under the mentioned restriction, becomes notably more comprehensive when no such limitation exists. Furthermore, this work also proves that the Einstein operator is a special case of the standard wave operator in curved spacetime by establishing a connection between them. This connection, in turn, leads to a novel proof that the standard wave operator in curved spacetime can be obtained from the Dirichlet operator for a manifold of variable signature. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our new approach, dubbed CTTK, offers a more feasible path for solving the constraints in such complex scenarios and significantly reduces the computational time required for solution refinement, compared to standard approaches. This improved performance is attributed to the direct solution of the conformal field equations, which eliminates the need for coarse-grained reconstruction of the metric variables. We further show that using this method in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition leads to equivalent results, but with a notable increase in convergence times. This new algorithm is an important breakthrough for the development of innovative strategies that could address the lingering issues of solution existence and uniqueness in the standard conformal field equations. This discovery is also expected to have a significant impact on the broader field of numerical relativity. This research was conducted while one of the authors was visiting the University of Oxford. This result establishes the first evidence for this decay mode at the level of $6.6 \sigma$ excess and estimates the branching fraction to be $(3.4 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-8})$. This rare occurrence cannot be accommodated by the Standard Model and its contribution to the $SU(3)$ flavour symmetry breaking is $\Delta\Gamma_{\mu\mu}/\Gamma_{\mu\mu}=(1.81\pm0.33) \times 10^{-3}$. Additionally, various momentum and kinematic distributions are presented with no notable features found in kinematic information either. The findings here are in line with theoretical expectations within the Standard Model. Furthermore, a likelihood ratio test for looking for a contribution from a scalar or vector resonance within the dimuon mass range finds no statistical evidence. Also, the paper reports on upper limits of excited $\Sigma$ or $\Lambda$ decay modes at masses below 8.9 GeV.

A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our experimental data also highlight the utility of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials as passive thermal management components. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the anomalous Nernst coefficient can be manipulated through the application of external electric fields, revealing new possibilities for the design of efficient thermal management technologies.   \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$. Additionally, when the obstacle function is not bounded, we establish results related to the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of a Sobolev space, where map $a$ belongs to a Hilbert-Schmidt operator, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$. A key component of our proof is the identification of a new function space, which is then utilized in conjunction with the potential theorem, an integral integral representation theorem and a chain rule, to derive conclusions about the differentiability of the solution. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Furthermore, we propose an environment-based remedy to overcome the difficulties encountered with anti-ferromagnetic interactions, a finding that could further the development of quantum-annealing-based solutions for complex optimization problems. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. The experiments conducted on three classification problems and one generative model scenario confirm the benefits of this approach. The findings show that by dividing the network into two layers, the accuracy is improved by at least 3.1%. Additionally, the proposed method surpasses the performance of the baseline model when the network is undivided, achieving an increase in accuracy of 0.7%. The results also indicate that, as the network depth increases in an unstructured manner, a 5% improvement in accuracy is achieved. The proposed method also successfully trains ResNet50 and Inception-V4, which couldn't be trained with the baseline method due to memory constraints. The findings also indicate that the proposed method achieves a significant increase in accuracy of 7.5% in an RNN setting, by training the network in a structured three-layer structure, which would have otherwise required over 400 million parameters. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The developed methodology's potential to contribute to the advancement of intelligent materials that can accurately detect a wide range of damages and sizes and shapes should be recognized.
However, there is a need for further research to be conducted on other type of damage like cracks in CNF-GFRP composites. 
Additionally, comparing the efficiency of this technique with other algorithms such as gradient-based methods or neural networks is also highly advised. 
Lastly, a more in-depth analysis of the effects of CNF concentration should be a consideration in the future research of this topic. 
The technique's effectiveness might be dependent on specific composite materials used and therefore more research is needed for different composite materials used in the study. 
More information about this research can be found in the paper "Precise Damage Shaping in Self-Sensing Composites Using Electrical Impedance Tomography and Gradient-Based Algorithms" that was recently published in the journal "Extreme Mechanics Letters". 
The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/AmirHoseinJafari/Code-for-Precise-Damage-Shaping-in-Self-Sensing-Composites.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework. The approach is then applied to demonstrate and prove identities related to geometric vector identities. Furthermore, potential applications and future research directions in this area are discussed. The approach is mathematically expressed as follows: Let $x$ represent a Euclidean space point described by coordinates $x_1, x_2,...,x_n$, and consider the geometric vector or scalar function $f(x)$ defined as the sum of its components $f_i(x_i)$ in the standard basis. With this understanding, any geometric vector or scalar function $f(x)$ may be transformed into the standard basis using the standard transformation $J_N$. Consequently, $f(x)$ is equivalent to the sum of its components in this basis, specifically $f_N$, and the relationship may be expressed as $f(x) = f_N(J_N x)$. This formulation enables the development of a tensor description for Euclidean spaces based on geometric vectors and provides a new perspective on the concept of reference systems in geometry. This approach is then utilized to redefine common geometric vector identities and create novel ones, accompanied by a brief exploration of potential applications. Furthermore, an uncontracted tensor description for Euclidean spaces is proposed and demonstrated through the redefinition of well-known geometric vector identities using this new framework. This has implications for both mathematics and physics, offering a fresh perspective on geometric algebra and suggesting its utility as an advanced educational topic that can showcase the benefits of index notation. This work also raises questions about the relationship between geometric and tensor descriptions, as well as the potential for further exploration in non-Euclidean spaces. This approach is then used to create an innovative geometric proof for an identity related to the volume of a parallelepiped in Euclidean spaces. This new proof may have value in teaching the fundamentals of geometry and the relationship between geometric and tensor notation. Building on this understanding, an identity related to the derivative of geometric vectors in Euclidean spaces is demonstrated and proved through this new approach. This research is accompanied by an educational component, which includes an appendix that provides an abstract introduction to geometric vectors and tensors suitable for undergraduate university students. This appendix defines geometric vectors and tensors, demonstrates their relationship, and shows how geometric vectors may be represented as tensors. Furthermore, it illustrates the connection between geometric and tensor notation, followed by a discussion on the potential benefits of teaching geometric algebra using index notation. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. Furthermore, the research suggests that elements of remote learning can enhance certain learning behaviors and these benefits may extend to other subjects and age groups. Consequently, the study recommends incorporating practical guidelines from successful online learning platforms to bolster the effectiveness of remote learning in university physics courses. Additionally, the research lays the groundwork for exploring ways to incorporate elements of remote learning into traditional classroom settings to create more adaptable and resilient learning environments. Finally, the investigation suggests potential avenues for further research, such as examining the long-term impacts of remote learning on physics retention and motivation, as well as the potential for online learning to mitigate the physical and mental health-related drawbacks of extended laboratory sessions. Moreover, the study implies that the incorporation of online learning modules can serve as an early warning system for identifying at-risk students and informing targeted supportive interventions. Lastly, the investigation highlights the significance of collaborative efforts among higher-education institutions to design and implement more effective remote learning platforms that cater to the needs of a diverse student population in physics and other subjects. The study's findings also emphasize the importance of prioritizing the well-being and academic support of university students during pandemic periods and beyond. The research

Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. Additionally, we find that the boundary complex of a building mirrors the structure of a biautomatic space when associated with a uniform lattice. This conceptual framework allows us to prove the conjecture recently posed by the researchers in the field. Furthermore, we observe that group extensions by isometries of buildings' boundary complexes also yield biautomatic groups. A key component of our proof involves establishing conditions under which the boundary complex's isometry group retains the biautomatic property. This condition is encapsulated within a condition known as the Local Accessibility Condition (LAC). We further illustrate examples to illustrate the prevalence of LAC among various types of buildings. A notable aspect of our theorem is the identification of a specific subset of buildings whose graph of apartments embodies a structure that is both locally accessible and locally transversable. As a result of which we are able to conclude that the graph of apartments for buildings such as Coxeter complexes, hypertree buildings, and certain type D buildings all satisfy the LAC, thereby leading to the conclusion that their associated uniform lattices also possess biautomatic structures. A detailed examination of our proof procedure reveals a method for constructing biautomatic structures within uniform lattices. A key aspect of our proof involves establishing a connection between the structure of a group extension and the structure of its kernel, thereby establishing a link between the graph of apartments and the group extension. A notable aspect of our research involves a comparison between the graph of apartments and the Deligne's building, which leads to a deeper understanding of buildings whose graph of apartments fails to satisfy the LAC condition. A conclusion of our research is the identification of several important issues related to graph of apartments, as well as some notable examples of buildings whose graph of apartments may either satisfy or fail to satisfy the LAC condition. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration. The discovered relationship allows for determining the new mass and charge configuration in a near-extremal black hole following the scattering process. The study also reveals that when a certain condition is met, the scattering cause an near-extremal black hole to retain its near-extremal properties. The results obtained from analyzing the scattering of a scalar field in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes can be applied to all such black holes, as their stability is not affected by the scalar field. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of recovering complex aspects of gait using a high-resolution invasive recording technique like ECoG, offering a promising avenue for the development of more advanced and reliable walking prosthetics. Additionally, this study's findings could be applied to other locomotion-based brain-control systems that rely on real-time step rate feedback. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. Our research sheds light on the statistical properties of each generator and offers insights into the selection of an appropriate generator to use in conjunction with Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. The results of our study are made available to the scientific community through the incorporation of our findings into the online Phylan database. This resource provides an up-to-date comparison of phylogenetic network generators, featuring information on each tool's performance, as well as the topological characteristics of the generated networks according to various criteria. Furthermore, the database enables users to execute a wide range of comparative analyses among the generators. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. The mathematical techniques employed can also be viewed from an optimization perspective, suggesting that declarative networks may offer a novel blend of deep learning and optimization-based modeling. The codes used in this research have been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghorpads/deepopt. The declarations and supplementary materials can be found in the appended files. The novel memory-efficient memory update scheme we introduced can be seen as an OTPrimal-smallest-path extension of the famous Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Furthermore, we have derived an accelerated version of this scheme, which can handle non-differentiable costs but still facilitates efficient Hessian-free updates. This accelerated scheme can be viewed as an OTFW algorithm. Both of these new algorithms have been comprehensively evaluated in multiple scenarios - both with synthetic and real-world data - in terms of their solution quality, runtime, and memory usage. The results have shown that the accelerated scheme generally yields better declarative network performance. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the complexity of this activation cascade, a comprehensive understanding of how it leads to the relocation of specific proteins is difficult to attain through experimentation alone. As a result, the development of a unified framework that can predict the behavior of these proteins is highly desirable. In this study, we introduce a mathematical framework that can model the activation of signaling pathways, the movement of lipid vesicles, and the relocation of proteins. This framework can be applied to study the behavior of particular protein responses in vitro and in vivo. As shown in this study, the movement of lipid vesicles and the activation of tyrosine kinases can be modeled using a system of nonlinear differential equations. Furthermore, the probability of a protein being activated can be calculated as a function of the vesicle's location, and the protein's relocation dynamics can be modeled using an advection-diffusion equation. This study also demonstrates the benefit of reducing the complexity of a given problem before attempting to model it, and the necessity of clear communication among researchers when translating biological concepts into mathematical models. In addition, it highlights the possibility of adapting the Duhem-Gagliardo theorem to derive the advection-diffusion equation from a nonlinear system of differential equations. This study's approach to modeling the behavior of individual cells can be extended to model the behavior of populations of cells. This extension holds promise for addressing more complex biological questions related to the behavior of cells in vitro and in vivo. As shown in this study, the behavior of individual cells cannot be predicted based on their average properties; rather, their behavior is influenced by the vesicles' advection and the activation of tyrosine kinases. Furthermore, this study's approach can be applied to model the behavior of migratory cells, such as neutrophils, by taking into account the activation of protein complexes and the breakdown of small molecules. Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide cost savings and optimal resource allocation.
However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on a larger scale.
Validation is conducted across multiple cloud providers and HPC systems, revealing that system noise and variability can substantially impact both performance and cost at both small and large scales. 
Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of accounting for network noise and potential for bottlenecks when designing and optimizing HPC systems for cloud deployment. 
In addition, it provides the basis for further exploration into methods to reduce network noise, such as network optimization and data transfer pattern adjustments, as well as the development of more precise models for predicting system behavior. 
Such advancements could enable more efficient and effective cloud HPC system design, deployment, and usage. 
In terms of practical applications, this study can facilitate better cloud HPC system configuration, leading to better performance, lower costs, and overall greater scalability. 
However, it should be noted that the research model described here is specifically tailored to address cloud HPC challenges and is not a general noise modeling approach. 
On the contrary, it distinguishes this model from other general noise modeling approaches. 
Furthermore, the term 'noise' used in this study holds a meaning that is opposite to its usual definition in mathematical and physical contexts. 
In those fields, noise refers to random fluctuations, whereas in this study, it represents the consistent, predictable variability of system components. 
As a result of these differences, this model-based research strategy should be recognized as an innovative approach, rather than a conventional one. 
In any case, further research is needed to fully validate and refine this model and its underlying assumptions with respect to system noise and variability. 
In the meantime, the name 'noise' used in this study may be seen as somewhat misleading in its conventional sense. 
Nonetheless, it has proven to be a beneficial and useful term in the context of this research. 
In conclusion, when designing and optimizing cloud HPC systems, it is essential to consider the inherent variability of system components, or system noise, as it can have a major impact on both system performance and costs at both small and large scales.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. Furthermore, our results indicate that both home working and Scrum use are essential for achieving personal growth, while Scrum use is linked to increased job satisfaction. Additionally, our model demonstrates the significance of both variables for project success, personal growth, and job satisfaction. Our theoretical contribution is an extended Self-Determination Theory (SDT) with additional components, and our study's findings have practical implications for both home working and Scrum practices. Our results encourage managers to adopt a combination of both home working and Scrum practices to facilitate project success, personal growth, job satisfaction, and overall well-being. Our study's limitations include the exclusion of non-software engineering projects and the reliance on a single data set. Future research could build upon this study by investigating additional project contexts, collecting data from multiple sources, or examining the impact of home working on Scrum projects over an extended period. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  The Event Shape Engineering technique confirms previous findings on the ratio of elliptic flow to radial flow and its dependence on transverse momentum.  Further, results show that the radial flow's energy dependence in the medium dynamic range is consistent with experimental data from smaller, lighter collisions.  Notably, results for particles with different masses indicate that the ratio of the elliptic flow to radial flow increases with the mean transverse momentum when considering identified particles.  Finally, results for inclusive spectra and flow coefficients are used to calculate initial entropy per unit volume, which is found to be 0.036±0.001 (sys) ± 0.001 (method) GeV/fm^3, consistent with other experimental data.  Additionally, the calculated ratio of entropy to energy density is 0.6±0.2, which is consistent with $\epsilon=0.6$ pb/GJ.  Results support the idea that matter created in heavy-ion collisions behaves as a quark-gluon plasma with properties consistent with its being a fundamental, collective medium.  Furthermore, the Event Shape Engineering technique's outcomes for elliptic flow and spectra are compatible with 3+1d relativistic hydrodynamic model simulations that simulate the behavior of a quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. Additionally, we provide a generalization of this factorization technique to the form $x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0$, encompassing various specific cases like the Fermat's little theorem, Pythagorean triples, and more. Furthermore, we derive an alternative proof involving the concept of a polynomial ring's Euclidean division, in accordance with division algorithm principles. Lastly, we demonstrate that any solution to the given congruence can be expressed as an intersection of two respective subgroups within the unit circle of the complex plane, thereby enabling a novel geometric interpretation of its elements. This interpretation is then applied to derive novel sets of congruence relations in relation to $a$ and $b$. Finally, we explore possible generalizations of these results across broader mathematical contexts. To this end, we formulate two specific conjectures on the divisibility properties of certain polynomials, following the principles of both our initial proof and geometric interpretation. These conjectures, if proven, would yield far-reaching generalizations of our findings and potentially new insights into various theoretical areas. Although we are unable to arrive at a definitive conclusion on these conjectures at this time, we are confident that our work will still provide a valuable contribution to the broader field of mathematics. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was then developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This research has implications for the optimal design of foot pads in legged locomotion on yieldings terrain. A economic design problem for foot pads was then presented, but unfortunately, cannot be optimized using nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques due to issues with parallelization. A potential remedy involves modifying the optimization algorithm itself. Three alternative algorithms are presented as potential solutions. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. This research aims to unveil the hidden capabilities of this droplet, specifically its ability to generate circulatory patterns in an aerosol environment, a feature that the researchers refer to as a "droplet electrohydrodynamic blower." This concept could have the potential to expand our understanding of various phenomena, such as the vaporization of droplets in different environments and the dispersion of particles. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our CONDAQA dataset offers novel assessments of a language model's capability to grasp negation, a skill considered essential for any sophisticated language capability. Despite the relatively recent study of negation in language, our evaluation results indicate that many current models continue to struggle with this aspect. Our findings are further validated by attempts to relate the challenges encountered in CONDAQA to those present in other complex reasoning tasks, such as Abductive Reasoning, Inference, and Executive Functions, both through human evaluations and the incorporation of auxiliary tasks. Our CONDAQA dataset serves as a pioneering reading comprehension dataset that poses a range of complex challenges to any NLP system claiming to master comprehensive language capabilities. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Furthermore, HDTM's capabilities were substantiated through a user survey, revealing that the generated hierarchies are not only computationally accurate but also coherent from a semantic perspective. By leveraging a reductionist approach and combining document-level and topic-level processing, HDTM delivers hierarchies that are not only semantically sound but also efficiently computable for large documents and datasets. These innovations demonstrate the potential of our approach to enhance both the usability and effectiveness of interactive systems operating within complex information networks. By consolidating multiple topics into organized layers, HDTM provides both a unified framework for compressing intricate data and a powerful tool for discovering hidden patterns in complex networks. As our experiments show, HDTM excels in scaling to massive data sets, outperforming both latent Dirichlet allocation and hierarchical matrix factorization in terms of model convergence speed and memory usage. By modeling documents as interrelated components rather than isolated entities, HDTM paves the way for more comprehensive and accurate understanding of complex information networks. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench gap that forms after the Hamiltonian change, across which exchanging the order of the qubit operations restores symmetry. Additionally, combining multiple quench gaps following varying annealing schedules leads to the same optimal solution, suggesting that quench studies can offer insights into the annealing gap and potentially enhance quantum annealing performance. A new 'quantum annealing trajectory' followed by a quench in the opposite direction is proposed, leading to the localization of the ground state within a surprisingly short time frame, even for larger-scale exact cover problems. A connection between the quench gap and the annealing schedule is established, along with a new 'quench schedule' that results in gap minimization, showing that both quantum annealing and quenching can be optimized and that they share a common underlying physics. A new 'quantum annealing trajectory' followed by a reverse quench in the opposite direction of qubit operations is proposed in order to reduce the gap, and this protocol is applicable to various types of the exact cover problem. Furthermore, incorporating a non-stoquastic mixture of Hamiltonians into the quantum annealing process, as well as the addition of an erase step to the protocol, both lead to significant improvements in gap minimization. A proposed experiment involves combining quantum simulation and digital annealing to study the quantum annealing gap. Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. Specifically, it develops two new techniques for analyzing incomplete process runs, compares them to existing methods, and provides guidelines for selecting the most appropriate alignment algorithm for different scenarios. Furthermore, the paper is accompanied by an openly available and easily usable library for conducting alignments with event data, called Aladdin. This event data analysis library can be utilized with popular process model properties and various alignment algorithms, making it a versatile tool available under an open-source license. Additionally, the paper includes results from a variety of process conformance checks involving real-world event data, including video footage of process runs with multiple doctors and a leading Dutch healthcare organization, and is accompanied by an appendix with additional technical details. This research was presented at the BPM 2022 conference in Italy. Finally, the paper's accompanying library can be found at https://github.com/utwente-apn/aladdin and its user guide at https://www.cs.rutgers.edu/~asilge/AladdinGuide.pdf. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, this study demonstrates that the diverse range of one-band physics
observed in infinite layered nickelates can all be explained through a single
two-band model.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Furthermore, our research can serve as a reference for those interested in exploring the context of Twitter datasets. The underlying sentiment of each feature was first identified through the application of multiple machine learning classifiers, including decision trees, logistic regression, naive bayes, and SVM. Subsequently, the most accurate classifier was selected and the underlying sentiment of the dataset was determined. Thereafter, the dataset was utilized to train a linear regression model, and the context of the dataset was learned based on the identified sentiment. The employed sentiment analysis resulted in the evaluation of Twitter datasets from India and Italy, utilizing 6000 samples each. Among these, 70% of the data was employed for training and the remaining 30% for testing. The accuracy of the classification was found to be 87% for India and 85% for Italy. The underlying sentiment of the India dataset was found to be positive, while that of the Italy dataset was found to be negative. A linear regression model was then applied to the datasets of India and Italy, with the aim of learning their context. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. This anti Tai mapping concept can be seen as a counterpart to the classic Tai mapping, and its computational algorithm may be useful in resolving Tai mapping-related optimization problems. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As a result, we found that VSI's development is impeded by increasing particle sizes in a range extending from 1 millimeter to 1 meter in diameter. Furthermore, in a report to be presented at the 39th meeting of the American Astronomical Society, we discuss our model's underlying premises and its underlying framework.

Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates and nonlinear Schrödinger equations, have a self-accelerating counterpart in higher dimensional space. This paper explores and proves the existence and stability of these self-accelerating solitons for certain fundamental models, including the one-dimensional Dirac equation, the one-dimensional Maxwell-Chern-Simons model, and certain nonlinear Schrödinger equations. It also demonstrates that in two-dimensional space, some of these models can support two self-accelerating solitons. Our research was guided by the properties of one- and two-dimensional solitons and was largely inspired by previous work on BEC physics. However, our findings can be applied to a broader range of theories and contexts. For example, some of these models have equivalents in the instanton calculus of $\cal N$=4 super-Yang-Mills theory, and could potentially be relevant to non-relativistic, two-dimensional self-accelerating fluids like planar superfluids. We also show that some of these models can support self-accelerating solitons in higher dimensional space, provided that a symmetry is enforced, and that these solutions can be interpreted as bound states of monopole-antimonopole pairs. Additionally, we demonstrate that a particular one-dimensional self-accelerating soliton can be viewed as an isolated point-like structure, and that some of these models can support self-accelerating solitons that result from the combination of two distinct one-dimensional self-accelerating states. Finally, we note that while some of these models can support self-accelerating solitons, they do not necessarily provide the most general or widest-ranging implications for the underlying theory. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This is achieved by introducing an inequality constraint on the communication costs, leading to a linear programming problem that can be solved efficiently. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Building on previous work by Hörmander, we demonstrate that the given property of $P$ being elliptic is both necessary and sufficient. Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when the number of items is large in comparison to the rounding level. When the underlying distribution is known and the variables are independent, we investigate how to calculate the expected value and variance of the original variable, even if the distribution is unknown. We applied these findings to analyze the effect of rounding on testing hypotheses concerning population means and proportions. We also developed a general approach for obtaining moments of a distribution, given a rounded version of the data. This resulted in us being able to reexamine research on the effect of rounding when testing proportions. Finally, we discuss ways to deal with rounding in general, beyond just averaging, and explore potential new testing procedures. We also offer our data and a user-friendly guide for following our methodology. If we can generalize our approach, it may lead to insights on other research questions. Rounding is an common practice and understanding its impact could be useful in many areas.

Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. This represents a notable improvement of over 20% when compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques on the ReID task. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. For the region of quark masses tested, which aligns with the physical point, the chiral perturbation theory calculations accurately predict the expected outcomes for the normalization and shape of the correlation function. Nonetheless, our research reveals that quark mass dependence in the correlation function is more intricate than anticipated and deviates from the expectations of the $\text{SU}(2)$ Nambu-Goldstone boson exponentiation. Additionally, our study offers the first concrete evidence for the relevance of the Wigner mode in the pion's structure, specifically in the U4 sector, where the quark and antiquark exhibit distinct transformations under the chiral flavor symmetry. This distinction results in the separation of the correlation function into two distinct components, with one component matching the pion's properties and the other component representing a flavor-exotic state that shares the same mass as the pion but with different resonance properties. This exotic state is then designated as the Wigner mode partner of the pion, with the name $\text{h}^\pi$. The emergence of this exotic state in our research represents a fundamental aspect of QCD and an inherent property of the light quark's interaction, with potentially far-reaching implications for other lattice QCD simulations. Furthermore, our results suggest that the existence of this exotic state may be corroborated through other lattice simulations that focus directly on the evaluation of the correlation function in question. If so, this would entail a significant breakthrough in our understanding of the pion's internal structure and the underlying principles of the strong force. Lastly, our findings indicate that the quark field combinations associated with the U4 sector play a crucial role in the pion's properties, with potential implications for the interpretation of experimental data derived from processes involving the conversion of photons to hadrons, as seen in the conversion of photons to hadrons in the study of muon decay. This, in turn, may lead to a revision of the current theoretical predictions for these processes. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. This paper introduces a new sampling-based approach that efficiently computes the Shapley value for training examples within a unified machine learning pipeline framework. The proposed method is experimentally evaluated on various pipeline configurations, models, and datasets, showcasing its computational benefits and diagnostic insights. The research outcomes indicate that the new method outperforms existing alternatives by yielding more accurate debuggings and substantially reducing the computational time. The newly introduced framework, along with a sample code, is made publicly available to support future research in data debugging. The paper's contributions, including its findings and practical applications, are discussed in the context of artifical intelligence. Furthermore, potential future research directions for the proposed framework are also highlighted. The paper is published as a conference paper at the 2022 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Safety. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has learned to exploit a game loop, while the other has mastered a skill, existing offline methods can result in the team performing poorly. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality, individual trajectories and encourage sharing of effective experiences among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex offline multi-agent games, especially in scenarios with significant variations in the quality of individual trajectories. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our research highlights the significance of continuing observations that will ultimately allow for the direct identification of Population III mergers. Furthermore, the impending creation of the Extremely Large Telescopes will offer the opportunity to detect Population III remnants directly, making timely predictions based on our model's framework. Additionally, we outline potential signs that could indicate the detection of a Population III merger and foresee future advancements in detector sensitivity and the potential for the direct detection of Population III binaries. Nonetheless, even with the improvement in detector sensitivity, the majority of enhanced detections may not be attributed to Population III events as predicted by this model. Therefore, the assignment of detected events as Population III mergers will rely heavily on the performance of current and future generation of multi-messenger observations and telescopes.
