Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's scientific knowledge base correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge compares to that gained from published findings. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, establishing a measure of knowledge progress in each field. Ultimately, they found that the increase in new knowledge surpasses the growth of published literature in most areas, yet this additional knowledge does not necessarily translate to a greater disparity between existing knowledge bases or a greater difference in the knowledge gained from new publications. Furthermore, they discovered that the overall knowledge base of a discipline is more susceptible to decline than the progress of new knowledge or the difference made by new publications. Additionally, they identified various disciplines where the threat of decline in existing knowledge or new progress outpaces the growth of new knowledge or the difference made by new publications. Lastly, they propose that the most critical factor influencing the value of new knowledge or literature is the reputation of the author or publisher, rather than factors such as the prominence of the journal or the quantity of citations. This research provides a framework for creating a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationship between scientific productivity and the growth of knowledge, a resource that other research can draw upon. The findings presented can be used to inform strategies for optimizing the discovery of literature, promoter programs, or initiatives that reward authors for their contributions, among other applications. The methodology is also a model for replicable and reproducible research within the knowledge domain. The data and analysis methods developed can be used to investigate the same research questions in other knowledge domains. The techniques employed for the citation analysis are also a demonstration of the benefits of using specialized tools, such as General Graph-Based Node Embeddings, over more general methods. The comparison of the performance of different models for the citation task highlights the significance of tailoring the technique to the characteristics of the network being analyzed. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
We discovered that evaluating virtual agents in text understanding tasks is surprisingly robust and unaffected by the increased simulation speed, while expert players' abilities are notably impacted, with them performing considerably better under more realistic conditions. 
In particular, we found that removing artificial limitations from the games can actually make them easier for human players and agents relying on rule-based approaches, though adding artificial advantages can still give them a significant boost. 
Finally, we incorporated additional features into the games that can be quickly scaled up or modified with minimal programming effort, largely due to the use of advanced tools like PyTSCII and Parsec, which streamlined the development process and quickly integrated our improvements back into the games. 
Overall, our research highlights the value of updating older text-based games to take advantage of more advanced simulation technologies, which can provide a more realistic and challenging setting for evaluating the performance of virtual agents. 
The updated TextWorldExpress games, along with their source code and instructions on how to use them, are available at https://github.com/AtsushiSakai/TextWorldExpress. 
Our research also included a study on the effectiveness of yet another highly-optimized text-based game challenge called Minigrid, which we used as a starting point but ultimately found to be less effective than TextWorldExpress in meeting our stringent performance standards. 
As a result, we highly recommend using the more advanced and faster TextWorldExpress games instead of simpler alternatives like Minigrid or even original old-school text games.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. In particular, the FDHT-LSTM architecture has been successfully applied to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the ActivityNet dataset, the first time a deep learning-based method has achieved top results on this dataset. Overall, this research demonstrates the potential of algorithm and hardware co-design to deliver high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks that can accurately analyze complex time-series data. The customized hardware designs developed here, specifically the FDHT-LSTM unit, also provide a valuable framework for the design of various deep learning components that can be applied to various application-specific hardware platforms. The expertise gained from working on the ActivityNet dataset, which involves high-dimensional data and therefore presents significant challenges for deep learning-based methods, can be applied to other large-scale datasets across various domains with great success. The unique approach to designing hardware and algorithms concurrently has enabled the creation of innovative solutions such as the FDHT-LSTM unit, which has the potential to propel the development of various deep learning technologies in multiple domains. The expertise and knowledge gained from the work on the ActivityNet dataset can also be applied to other large-scale datasets across various domains with great success. The paper presents novel algorithmic innovations like the FDHT-LSTM structure, pioneering hardware designs such as the customized FPGA board that incorporates a sophisticated memory access scheme, and groundbreaking evaluation results on the ActivityNet

This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. In simulations and calculations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in terms of convergence. Notably, we find that folded-spectrum QITE converges to the quantum minimum energy state within that range. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The study provides actionable advice for policy makers and market designers to enhance market performance and mitigate negative consequences when developing redispatch policies and market designs. The model's versatility allows it to be applied to various regional power landscapes, such as the German electricity grid, and can be adapted to accommodate a wide range of design choices and policy settings. The model's design also facilitates the exploration of novel market designs, such as side-payment mechanisms in multi-period redispatch, which is a promising area for future policy research. The model is available at https://github.com/energydatagroup/Ancillary-Services-Acquisition-Model, and is maintained by the Energy Data Group at https://www.energydatagroup.com/. The model relies on PyPSA-Python, an open-source Python framework for Power System Analysis, developed by the Energy Data Group, and is available at https://www.pypsa3.org/. The model has been created through a collaboration between the University of Sussex, the University of Oxford, and the Technical University of Denmark. The model's development has been supported by the European Commission's Horizon 2020 programme, specifically through the H2020 EERA-Jazz Partner Council

Our proof relies on a groundbreaking theorem from the works of Bhargava and Stroup, and it expands upon earlier research from the works of Annoni, Cluckerman, Brightman, and Papanikolaou. Our findings also offer a characterization of the set of local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings in terms of local positive-characteristic reductions. As a result, we establish a correspondence between the former set and the latter set, or a non-trivial subgroup of the latter set, which is highly intricate and likely vast. This correspondence holds the potential to shed light on fundamental questions in number theory, specifically questions related to the distribution of prime numbers and the nature of varieties. Our proof of this correspondence for polynomial varieties will serve as a key component in the extension of this theory to more general varieties. Furthermore, we outline a general strategy for extending this proof to such broader varieties. Additionally, we outline additional consequences and potential research directions resulting from this proof. The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition in bulk V$_2$O$_3$.  These discoveries are further evidenced by a strong correlation between the metal-insulator transition and the hybridization of V $3d$ and O $2p$ states.  Our research offers a comprehensive explanation for the varied results reported in previous studies on V$_2$O$_3$ films and pinpoints the effect of surface termination, also providing a theoretical explanation to reconcile the observed results with those from bulk and lattice-matched film studies.  Our work lays the groundwork for a greater understanding of the intricate interplay between correlation physics and surface and interface effects in transition metal oxides.  Finally, our research may also provide a solution to the challenge of achieving a desired metal-insulator transition in these materials by deliberately engineering the correlation between electrons within these materials.  This can be accomplished by varying the distance between transition metal ions, for which there is a direct causal link with the effect of surface termination on V$_2$O$_3$ films as reported in our studies.  In essence, our findings demonstrate the feasibility of designing transition metal oxide films with optimal electronic properties by carefully controlling the surface termination.  This breakthrough discovery may also be applied to other complex oxide systems.  In order to validate our theoretical model, our research included a combination of experimental and theoretical analysis of V$_2$O$_3$ films conducted at the SLS and was a collaborative effort between the EPFL and the PSI. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, states with low condensate fractions may be more complex and difficult to model. We also provide an exact finite-size scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states. This includes a logarithmic correction term for large but not infinite system sizes, and it confirms the conjecture of Simmermacher and Rittenhouse. Additionally, our studies at finite but large system sizes should aid in designing future experiments to identify quasi-condensation in quantum double dark-soliton states. We further investigate the relationship between quantum and classical double dark-soliton dynamics. We demonstrate that the time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state can be represented as the product of an amplitude and a phase component, and that this composition follows a closed orbit in phase space. We then establish a direct connection between the amplitude and phase components of a quantum double dark-soliton state and those of a classical double dark-soliton state. We show that the phase component plays a crucial role in the composition of a quantum double dark-soliton state and that it cannot be ignored in any analysis of these states. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Furthermore, this method may be adapted for application with larger sources like laboratory-based x-ray setups. The new algorithm's effectiveness is shown with experiments involving the measurement of time-domain M\"ossbauer spectra, a landmark study that contributes significantly to the field of x-ray optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy. The algorithm's development of beneficial data analysis tools represents a significant step towards a more comprehensive understanding of the phase and amplitude of x-ray scattering off nuclei, a new level of insight that could also be applied to the study of atomic and molecular processes with light. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. By modeling the impact of faulty parity checks and single-qubit errors, we also discuss the potential applications of this framework to other quantum codes. Additionally, we introduce a new concept called the "circuit noise universality class" to categorize different fault patterns based on their relative error magnitudes, and demonstrate how this framework can be used to analyze more complex circuits, such as quantum computation circuits, by representing them as combinations of elementary universal quantum gates. Furthermore, based on the classical spin models developed, we discuss the possibility of cross-checking theoretical predictions with experimental simulations of quantum error correcting circuits, utilizing photochemical reactions as an example of such a simulation. This involves discussing two possible approaches to extending this model-based analysis to multiple qubit errors and discussing the potential for experimenting with small-scale quantum circuits under controlled noise conditions. Finally, we consider how this framework can be adapted to deal with different types of quantum error, by exploring the potential for modeling the impact of faulty single-qubit unitary operations, and discuss the potential advantages of using this approach to study quantum error correcting circuits, particularly in relation to classical models of disordered systems. This includes a discussion of how this framework can be used to answer fundamental questions about the performance of quantum error correcting codes, and the potential for this to inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures, frames the problem as an mixed variational inequality, and demonstrates its main advantage to be locally conservative. Our approach also facilitates the use of multiple techniques for handling blocking fractures, including limiting the pressure on such fractures, developing a corresponding mapping method, and imposing constraints through the normal component of the velocity. A notable benefit of these new methods is the blocking fractures' ability to be irregularly shaped. Several numerical tests have been conducted to verify our approach's accuracy and efficiency. These tests include diverse blocking fractures' configurations, up to three intersecting blocking fractures, and a scale-invariant simulation. Our research provides a groundbreaking direction for future research on multi-phase flow in fractured media. The corresponding code is made accessible upon request. Additionally, an open-source code based on this approach is currently being developed and is also available for consideration and improvement.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics that may arise due to competing isotropic exchanges or an asymmetrical magnetic arrangement. Depending on its anisotropy, the metal can transition between spiral and uniform magnetization orders. A specific type of magnetic arrangement known as the B20 structure further contributes to the device's operation, influencing the long-range pairing of superconducting electrons under intense exchange fields. However, numerical simulations demonstrate that an unusual orientation-dependent effect can be utilized to control the device's behavior at moderately low exchange fields. Consequently, a significant amplification of the device's effect is achieved when specific parameters such as exchange splitting and spiral period are comparable to the superconducting coherence length. A scenario involving a Co-based spiral layer paired with an Ni-based non-magnetic layer exhibits an exceptionally amplified device effect, outperforming its counterparts by an order of magnitude. This finding suggests that a simple superconducting spin-triplet valve can be devised using a single spiral magnetic layer. The results presented can be utilized to design such devices and their associated unique phenomena. Furthermore, the discovery of a spiral metal's capacity to support both ferromagnetic ordering and superconductivity may lead to further exploration of its properties. A brief discussion on the possibility of utilizing the spiral metal in a device is included at the end. The accompanying supplementary material delves into the technical aspects of the numerical simulations, the used model, and the metal's underlying magnetic energy profile. It also discusses the distinctive characteristics of the B20 structure and its impact on the device's operation. The supplementary material further expands on the possibilities of utilizing the spiral metal in a device, the unique energy profile of the metal, and the utilized numerical simulations. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts, the properties of cognitive models, and the qualifications of model parameters. We explore various complications, including model mismatch, the impact of prior distributions, and the issue of model selection in the presence of multiple alternative theories. We also discuss the benefits of an unbiased approach when reporting Bayes factor results, as well as the value of pre-registering analyses and data before completion, and the type of information that should be recorded in this process. We refer to this approach as 'robust Bayesian analysis,' and describe strategies for managing the results of such analyses, including the use of credit assignment methods to evaluate the performance of computational models in an unbiased manner. We apply this framework to a representative example drawn from the literature on human learning, and highlight the kind of information that can be gained from the analysis of Bayes factor results when cognitive models are subjected to rigorous evaluation methods. We anticipate that our proposals will contribute to the development of a more rigorous approach to comparative evaluation in cognitive science, and will facilitate the exchange of ideas between researchers who compare theories using Bayes factor analysis. We also hope that our work will help to establish clear guidelines for the use of computational models, and will provide a framework for addressing methodological complications that arise when analyzing the results of experiments on human and non-human subjects. We discuss the potential for our framework to be expanded to other fields that use computational models to analyze the results of experiments on human and non-human subjects, and the potential for our approach to be combined with other methods for evaluating the performance of computational models. We conclude by highlighting the key challenges that need to be addressed by the field, and the potential for our approach to contribute to the development of a more rigorous approach to the design of experiments and the analysis of data. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  This research may have implications for the development of nitrogen-vacancy-based sensing technologies in harsh environments.  To validate our results, we performed additional experiments under high-pressure conditions at room temperature, and our data also showed a correlation with the Mott-Seitz model.  This includes a observation of an unusual heat distribution effect on the ODMR frequencies, which may provide a more precise method of measuring high temperatures in small temperature ranges.  Furthermore, by controlling the intensity of the excitation, we were able to recover the typical nonradiative phonon-assisted behavior below a certain temperature threshold.  This includes a detailed phonon mode analysis, which could be of use in NV-diamond thermometry in certain applications.  Finally, we explore the possibility of using nitrogen-vacancy centers as sensitive probes of their surroundings, which could be critical for the development of NV-diamond as a robust and reliable sensing technology.  This includes a discussion of the importance of thoroughly understanding the interaction between the nitrogen-vacancy center and its surroundings under a variety of conditions, which could be achieved through the development of a more general and comprehensive theoretical model of NV-diamond behavior. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. The new HF method demonstrates the benefits of a straightforward algorithm and minimal requirement for memory, making it a practical and viable option for further studies of electron clusters. The source code of the new method has been openly shared and is suitable for use with central potentials. The code is primarily designed for single-node, single-processor operations, but it can also support parallel processing with the Message Passing Interface. The code is written in C, with some Fortran90 components, and is compatible with most central potential formats, including those based on numerical data files, analytical functions, and potential derivatives. The code is executable on a range of platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. The new HF method can also handle artificial central potentials, such as the'swallowtail' potential, which presents a challenge for established Roothan-HF algorithms. The results obtained with the new implementation are accurate, as verified through comparisons with established theories and experiments, and the method can be applied to a wide range of electron clusters, including atoms, ions, electron gas, and alkali-metal clusters. The development of further variants based on this new HF method is also described, including the B-spline local density approximation and the B-spline extension of the local Hartree-Fock method. The performance of these variants was validated through additional benchmark tests, and the results show that they can achieve accurate and efficient solutions of real and complex electronic systems within the scope of the new HF method. The development of the new HF method has made it possible to investigate the behavior of real and complex electronic systems from the perspective of time-independent Schrödinger equations, and the results obtained with this method are consistent with established theories and experiments. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems. Additionally, our findings may also facilitate the discovery of unanticipated explosive synchronization phenomena in response to various levels of internal disorder. As a demonstration of its utility, this research also identifies a novel instance of explosive synchronization within a widely used and extensively studied dataset of brain activity. This includes ECoG recordings from both humans and an animal model with further confirmation of its underlying dynamics using both numerical simulations and analytical solutions of its reduced model. This discovery could potentially provide a biologically based explanation for the observed benefits of specific brain states related to optimal memory performance. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, we incorporate an inexact gradient descent framework to demonstrate the almost sure convergence of sequences that enter the geodesically convex region. This study provides a theoretical foundation for the practical success of simple algorithms in nonconvex matrix factorization problems. Additionally, it implies that fixed-rank matrix optimization with a least squares objective can be cast as a geodesically convex optimization problem, extending an existing result for matrix factorization with a least squares objective when the factorization is full-rank. This research is a significant expansion on prior work and is a crucial step for addressing more complex matrix optimization problems under positive semidefinite constraints. Finally, we outline potential future directions for this line of research.

Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In addition, we observed that the "population size" parameter influenced the speed of convergence, but not the ability to converge, while the "fitness selection intensity" parameter affected the degree of convergence. Our research provides further evidence for the utility of co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in modeling players' strategic behavior in games of complete information. We have made our code publicly available to facilitate replication and extension of our research in future studies. To facilitate further investigation, we develop and release a publicly accessible tool for analyzing the behavior of evaporating droplets in various settings. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. This approach is demonstrated through a symbolic solver implemented in the Ratslaba system, an extension of the existing Ratsemu toolkit. Further, we show that our approach leads to a more efficient containment assessment algorithm and validate our method with a range of examples. Additionally, this research is part of a broader framework for the co-design of regular expression theories and implementation techniques. In contrast to the existing approach, which focuses on the automata-based containment assessment method described in reference [9], we explore alternative strategies for containment assessment, considering methods like the Boolean matrix multiplication containment assessment method mentioned in reference [10]. This new approach for containment assessment with regular expressions and sets of recognizable characters provides several advantages over the automata-based method, which has limited applicability due to its restrictive character set requirements. Nonetheless, both approaches have their own strengths and weaknesses, and there is potential for further research into containment assessment with regular expressions and sets of recognizable characters. Furthermore, this new approach may also be of interest for the study of formal languages and the development of implementable regular expression theories. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Furthermore, our proposed model achieves this pose estimation accuracy with only a fraction of the parameters compared to the recurrent models, showcasing its superiority. The model's code is available online at https://github.com/Heng-XY/EMA-VIO. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Notably, the hinge states in SHOWS can be manipulated through infrared light, enabling the practical observation of this phenomenon. This discovery not only expands our understanding of topological quantum mechanics but also opens up opportunities for creating novel photogalvanic effects in solid-state systems. This concept can also be extended to other higher-order topological phenomena in 3D systems. By applying this knowledge to design exotic topological materials, we can unleash the potential of showpieces of physics, like SHOWS, to facilitate unprecedented interactions between light and matter. Consequently, this discovery gives birth to a new class of solid-state systems that can harness light-matter interactions in unprecedented ways, providing fresh opportunities for advancing the field of quantum electronics. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. Simulation examples highlight the method's capability in handling smooth and non-smooth solutions, as well as its ability to tackle noisy data issues. The method is shown to preserve the original problem's physical properties, including conservation of energy. The approach is found to be robust, producing consistent results across multiple mesh configurations and demonstrating only minor sensitivity to the choice of discretization parameters, particularly the mesh size. The method is further found to be compatible with existing boundary conditions, such as perfect conductive conditions, and there is potential for extending the approach to other partial differential equation-based applications. The implementation of the method is straightforward, using established and well-documented software libraries. The method is currently being further developed to address the related problem of electric impedance tomography. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Furthermore, FedSA boasts enhanced communication efficiency, with each communication round consisting of only 8 unique model parameters, in contrast to 100-300 parameters in traditional federated learning. We have made all model codes and data available at: https://github.com/hjdw2/FedSA. Our innovative FedSA approach may also serve as a starting point for other creative ways to share model data. In the FedSA scenario, we combine our approach with Kornelius+, a customizable code that allows for the incorporation of diverse teacher networks available at https://github.com/hjdw2/Kornelius. This code is adaptable to various frameworks and can be modified to accommodate various network architectures. We have successfully executed FedSA using both PyTorch and TensorFlow. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. As a result, we suggest that observational indicators, such as star-spot patterns and magnetic field strengths, be used to differentiate between rotational regimes in slow rotators, thereby providing insight into the dynamos operating within these stars. This, in turn, can further contribute to our understanding of global magnetic processes occurring in solar-type stars across various rotational states. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings for PPLE simulations that account for magnetic cycles in a sample of 10 slow rotators. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of using mid-frequency transparency to nonlocally determine the local carrier concentration and dielectric characteristics. We found that our approach can also be adapted for studying dielectric properties in stri-line resonators. Overall, this study highlights the value of near-field terahertz investigations in understanding the local properties of materials within narrow features and layers, information that is not readily obtainable through far-field measurements. However, the practical implementation of these systems is hindered by two primary sources of decoherence: the lossy silicon substrate and the conductive metal components, which result in the unnecessary absorption of photons. While various methods have been proposed to address this issue, such as the use of gapless superconductors, there is still a need to thoroughly understand the carrier dynamics within these systems, particularly in the terahertz regime, in order to optimize the performance of quantum processors. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is a contribution to the NASA's Accessible Compact Astrobotany Laboratory (ACAL) and the NASA Venus Instrumentation Working Group (VIWG) efforts.

The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. Furthermore, the scalability of this method is demonstrated by applying it to a more challenging scenario involving the subtyping of whole breast tissue sections. The code and data for this project are made publicly available to contribute to the growth of the digital pathology community. The proposed HACT framework may also find utility in other spatially-organized tissue structure learning tasks. The potential of this approach to enhance the accuracy of cancer diagnosis and treatment plans is also discussed. In addition to its practical applications, the HACT framework's innovative architecture, centered around the integration of cell and tissue region features, may spark interesting discussions in the graph neural network community. The potential of this approach to be expanded to other domains, such as gene expression analysis, is also explored. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified theoretical framework based on the Wess-Zumino theory. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. Consequently, this is also applicable to supergravity, suggesting the necessity of formulating revised nilpotent transformations to accurately comprehend 3+1 dimensional supergravity. A potential approach to achieve this is by supplementing the auxiliary fields to incorporate the spin connection within a super Yang-Mills multiplet. A demonstration shows that the resulting theory is valid and consistent with empirical evidence, including the absence of a Fayet-Iliopoulos term. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however, a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. We then extend these training techniques to models that account for foreground contamination, the complexity of which often exceeds our ability to simulate their effects. As a result, the models often fail to accurately reconstruct the primordial gravitational wave signal, however, we were able to significantly improve this by incorporating an iterative foreground cleaning process. This led to delensing performance comparable to the best performing estimator, the neural network estimator with an iterative foreground cleaning process, often outperforming it when there is a relatively large non-zero primordial signal present. We also found that the neural network's delensing performance is highly dependent on several parameters such as the precision of the lensing reconstruction, the delensing iteration, and the foreground cleaning process, but it remains robust against variations in other parameters. Lastly, we found that the neural network's ability to learn from multiple iterations of its own processing allows it to achieve superior delensing performance when compared to the quadratic estimator and the maximum a posteriori estimator, however, we also found that this comes at the cost of significantly increasing the computational resources required, typically by two orders of magnitude over the quadratic estimator, however, it is still within the scope of what can be processed in a reasonable amount of time with the current computational power available to us. We hope this work will serve as a motivation for more research into the application of machine learning to the delensing problem, however, we also hope that the results presented here will serve as a benchmark against which the performance of any new method will be measured. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. This, in turn, has implications for the explosion energy and the mass of the compact remnant, which are expected to be a one solar mass black hole or a neutron star. We also explored the possibility of SN~2020jfo being explosion-powered by an unstable iron exponent ONS, but neutron star mergers are more plausible given the abundance ratio and other characteristics of this supernova. Lastly, we fit the light curve of SN~2020jfo with a variety of different relations including the generalised re-interpretation of the vector-modulus function, verifying that this supernova adheres to the standard Type II light curve behaviour and follows the trends established by other SNe~II. Additionally, we expanded the sample of type II supernovae with short plateau phases to which we fit a linear relation between the plateau duration and absolute peak magnitude, and SN~2020jfo's characteristics fit within the established patterns. Finally, we estimated the total absorbed energy up to day 434 for SN~2020jfo, and this, along with other metrics, makes this paper a comprehensive study on the Type II supernova SN~2020jfo.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The small size and lightweight nature of the MuLE optics make them well-suited for such applications. Additionally, the proposed MuLE design can be easily applied to other types of curved mirrors used in wide-field X-ray monitors. If successfully implemented, the MuLE optics could significantly reduce the total mass and volume of such monitoring systems by as much as a factor of 10. This could be particularly beneficial for future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The design's versatility also allows it to be modified for use in wide-field X-ray telescopes. The proposed MuLE design could potentially reduce the total mass and volume of such telescopes by as much as a factor of 10, which could be especially beneficial for future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The MuLE configuration could also be used in combination with a detector array consisting of multiple segments, each covered with a different sensitive material to detect variations in the X-ray energy spectrum. This could further enhance the capabilities of wide-field X-ray transient monitoring systems by detecting the energy spectrum of transient events. The proposed MuLE design could also be applied to the development of novel X-ray micro-calorimeter detectors with a large collecting area. These detectors, featuring multiple LEs, could be highly sensitive in detecting the energy spectrum of transient X-ray events and could be used in combination with the MuLE optics to further enhance the performance of wide-field X-ray transient monitoring systems. The MuLE optics design also offers the opportunity to develop novel X-ray interferometer systems consisting of multiple LEs, which could be used to monitor the intensity of X-rays as a function of time and could be beneficial in detecting transient X-ray events with a duration of seconds or longer

Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Notwithstanding this, our investigation reveals that CNMF's performance enhances with rising numbers of supervised examples, albeit at a slower rate than its fully supervised counterpart. To facilitate reproduction, our experiment is reproducible and all parameters are openly accessible online. Moreover, to mitigate overfitting often associated with low-rank factorization methods, we explored additional factorization techniques, including tensorized formats, which could be of broader interest to the music transcription community. Despite improving audio quality, our findings revealed that they yield inferior transcription results, likely resulting from inadequate representation of the musical notes within our proposed methods. One possible remedy could be incorporating an additional factorization layer, thereby enabling more precise representation of each musical note, thereby potentially mitigating the adverse effects on transcription accuracy. Ultimately, our exploration confirms that low-rank matrix factorization techniques, including CNMF, hold considerable promise for the development of next-generation piano transcription systems. To this end, our study's results, including all parameter settings and code, are now openly available on GitHub. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the extraction of five crucial social determinants of health factors - housing quality, transportation accessibility, meal availability, financial stability, and family support - which we refer to as the 'SDHevents' framework. We've developed and trained a unique, marker-based neural network system on the BioPortal corpus, an extensive collection of clinical notes derived from the University of Texas Health Science Center. Our system's performance was evaluated on two aspects: first, the ability to identify potential SDH events within clinical notes: and second, the overall accuracy of the extracted information. Our research indicates that our proposed method not only recognizes SDH events more effectively than existing state-of-the-art models but also enhances the precision of the extracted data. Furthermore, our findings provide actionable insights for future research in this domain. This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios. Notably, in the fastest time scenario, we find the optimal strategy involves switching at the point where the swimmer's shortest distance between configurations is half its total perimeter, dividing it into two equal parts. This optimal switching pattern allows the swimmer to complete one full cycle in a time of $\pi\sqrt{3L/(\mu_1 + \mu_2)}$ and achieves the best result for the least-cost scenario, indicating that optimizing the time or cost can both be solved by analyzing the underlying phase space and locating the optimal switching point. This understanding can be applied to a broader class of stochastic problems as shown in the appendix. Additionally, we explore how changing the parameters of the model, specifically the viscosity levels, affects the optimal performance. This analysis provides valuable insights into the optimal design of swimmer dynamics and control strategies within various fluid environments. We also examine the broader implications of our findings for more complex swimmers and discuss potential future research directions in this field. This study is an initial step in the comprehensive analysis of swimmers' optimal performance and control, and further investigation is needed to fully understand the complex interplay between the swimmer's dynamics, control strategies, and the surrounding fluid environment. Nonetheless, the results presented here clearly demonstrate the substantial improvements achievable through periodic control in optimizing a swimmers performance, and the simplicity of this approach makes it an ideal subject for collaborative research across disciplines. We hope this study will contribute meaningfully to those efforts. We have made available the code utilized for these analyses at https://github.com/ajtaylor-vt/optimal-scallop for anyone to access and build upon. Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner edge of the disk may not always result in a compact, optically thin accretion layer. Instead, it could also lead to the formation of irregular shapes that increase the disk's overall viscosity, facilitating mass transfer into the stellar body. This outcome is particularly common during the early stages of protostar development. It has also been observed that collisions between the protostar and its surrounding disk can produce irregular shapes that increase viscosity, resulting in enhanced accretion. This process, however, typically occurs at low viscosities (around $10^{-5}$), which could be improved by adding more robust disk interactions or by increasing the viscosity to $10^{-4}$. It's essential to note that these findings hold no dependence on the development of a hole within the disk, as previously suggested by researchers. It's proposed that the term "inside-out growth" be redefined to better fit the presented outcomes, and a distinction should be made between standard and high-viscosity disk development. It's also suggested that high-resolution simulations should investigate the growth of massive protostars under both idealized and unidealized conditions. It's estimated that in as little as $10^5$ years, a 10-solar-mass protostar could reach a mass of around 9 solar masses through accretion alone. It's also found that the merger of two objects of 1 solar mass each could add mass at a rate of up to 10$^{-5}$ solar masses per year. It's concluded that both episodic accretion and mergers could contribute noticeably to the growth of massive protostars. It's also proposed that the merger of more substantial objects could result in the formation of a longer-lasting disk that could facilitate continued mass transfer into the stellar body at a rate of up to 10$^{-4}$ solar masses per year for an extended period of time. It's also suggested that super-Eddington outflows could be triggered by the merger of two objects rather than accretion alone. It's also contended that both episodic accretion and mergers could result in the ejection of massive amounts of material at extremely high velocities, exceeding 100 km/s.

Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This suggests that accurate description of electron interactions is crucial for accurately modeling plasmon dynamics. This discussion on the limitations of local response models extends beyond gap plasmons, highlighting the widespread significance of a more comprehensive description of electron behavior. The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Our work also offers insights that can be applied to the study of other dependently typed programming languages with type dependence and type reconstruction. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the strong normalization property and the expressive power of a programming language. In particular, we investigate how the ability to define functions via recursion and fixed points in the type of dependently typed programming contributes to the achievement of the property of strong normalization. Our work is an expansion of the earlier research presented in the conference paper 'Dependent Types in Programming' also authored by the present researchers and presented at the 'Types in Type Theory' workshop in Copenhagen, Denmark. That research was previously presented as an extended abstract at the 'Homage to Gilles Kahn' workshop held in Paris, France. Our extended survey once again considers various means by which the property of strong normalization can be established for the Calculus of Constructions via the typing system itself, type checking, and dependency-driven typing, respectively. Our work has been designed to be an easily accessible introduction to this important research for which many readers may be searching. In addition, our research may also provide food for thought on this interesting topic. Last but not least, our work is an excellent example of how a survey on a research topic can be both a valuable resource for those learning about that topic and how a discussion on that topic can be enjoyable. We hope that this survey will be beneficial to all of our readers and that it will be enjoyable for at least some of our readers. Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMOO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  Additionally, we introduce the use of semi-static memory blocks in the DynaSOAr allocator, further enhancing memory management by reducing atomic operations, memory accesses, and conflicts, resulting in additional performance and memory access improvements of up to 3. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Additionally, the peculiar magnetic behavior of these defects could make TiO2 suitable for magnetic data storage applications.  Finally, we observed that the Liechtensstein method, an algorithm used to optimize anti-ferromagnetic arrangements, is highly effective in reducing the energy cost associated with such arrangements, and that a somewhat similar arrangement, the ferroelectric N-O dimer, could potentially be used to enhance TiO2's photocatalytic properties via tuning its band gap.  We hope that these predictions could potentially be validated and/or used in experiments.  Moreover, we suggest that in order to reduce costs, such experiments could be carried out on carbon-doped TiO2, as the theoretical outcomes are remarkably consistent with what is already known about nitrogen-doped TiO2.  Finally, we believe that the results presented here could potentially be applied to other doped semiconductors as well.  In conclusion, we have successfully used a hybrid DFT framework to investigate the electronic and magnetic structure of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  We have demonstrated that this approach results in a more accurate description of these systems when compared to alternative DFT methods.  Furthermore, we have utilized a 48-atom supercell to simulate these systems, and have validated our results against experimental data
