I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the neutrino-UHECR spatial correlations. These results remain sensitive to variations in magnetic fields influencing cosmic rays during their journey from sources to detectors. As such, further investigation will continue to be pivotal in resolving the origin of cosmic rays and neutrinos. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. We have also obtained evidence to support the idea that the stick-slip regime is associated with localized breaking within the Plateau border system. The findings of this study have implications for better understanding the flow of complex liquids and the role of surface roughness in various processes. Additionally, we have shown that friction in liquid foams can be manipulated by altering the type and amount of surfactant used. This knowledge could be adapted to improve the performance of technologies that utilize liquid foams in their operation. One such example is the "kickback" phenomenon experienced by some foam-based fire extinguishers. Understanding the factors that contribute to the stick-slip or stationary regimes could provide insights into potential solutions to mitigate the kickback effect. Lastly, we have demonstrated that the behavior of liquid foams shares some similarities with that of granular materials. While the issue of jamming has not been directly addressed in this study, we hope that our research could pave the way for a deeper exploration of this topic in the context of liquid foams. Additionally, we have offered some theoretical considerations to further elucidate the relationship between surface roughness and the different friction modes observed in our experiments. A greater comprehension of these phenomena could be acquired through numerical simulations that model the breakdown of shear bands and the occurrence of stick-slip motion. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the behavior of liquid foams could also provide valuable insights to researchers working on the study of glassy materials as well. One of the key takeaways from this research involves recognizing that surface roughness plays a significant role in determining the behavior of liquid foams. Furthermore, the behavior of these materials is dependent on the curvature of the Plateau borders, which are a unique feature of liquid foams that distinguish them from other complex liquids. The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. This size is found to be invariant with the rate of rotation and outer fluid density, and is instead determined by the balance of centrifugal and surface tension forces, resulting in a relationship with the Curvature-tension number previously observed in an identical setup with an inextensible interface. The influence of an increase in the inner fluid density relative to the outer fluid density is seen as a widening of the finger's base in proportion to the square of this ratio. A numerical model also demonstrates the potential for this system to produce multiple fingers in a quasi-periodic pattern. This analysis is further supported by a linear stability analysis and a non-dimensionalized model. A model for finger size relationships is validated through additional experiments. The findings of this study may also be applicable to an interface between two fluids with differing viscosities in a Hele-Shaw cell. The results of this study contrast with those of previous research on viscous interfaces in similar conditions, which indicated that the size of fingers in such situations increases with the rate of rotation. A model for costs associated with the production of food by fungal cultures could also be developed using a similar approach. This similar approach involves a comparison of the costs of extending the interface between two fluids with the costs of producing multiple structures in a semi-solid medium. A model for the size of these structures may be similar to that of a membrane in a Hele-Shaw cell, and could be applied to a bio-tech production process that involves the growth of a type of fungus in a viscous medium. This fungus produces enzymes that are then extracted from a liquid layer which is separated from the growth culture by an interface that is affected by the curvature and the viscosity of the liquids in a similar way to the membrane in a Hele-Shaw cell. A model for the cost of producing these enzymes could be developed using a similar approach. This model could be more cost-effective than a current model for the production of food by fungal cultures. A model for the size of structures produced in a similar way could also be developed using a similar approach.

However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Our approach also facilitates easier model interpretation by providing a means to identify target words with significant impacts on the attention weight. When applied to real-time applications, our proposed look-ahead attention reduces target sentence generation speed, but still outperforms the standard attention method. We also discuss the role of look-ahead attention in relation to source sentence attention and target word embedding, leading to a new insight that target word embedding can be viewed as a combination of two components: a language-model-inspired vector and a content-inspired vector. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. The model exhibits a past-deterministic behavior, which is crucial for its predictiveness. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation of state (EoS) and find that the model's EoS values are consistent with the existing data sets from the Hubble diagram, supernovae type Ia observations, cosmic microwave background radiation, recession velocity estimates from Hubble's law, and abundance of baryon acoustic oscillations. Our findings also support a universe with a present-day Hubble constant of approximately 71.86 km/s/Mpc. Our model successfully explains the present-accelerated and past-decelerated states of the universe and predicts a big bounce solution for its early universe. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  Our work has been tested with both simulated and real users, and the resulting technologies have shown improved curiosity levels and better performance.  In contrast to existing approaches that concentrate on individual learners, our research introduces a novel methodology for analyzing curiosity in groups and identifying the underlying structures that govern curiosity dynamics. While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, will enable graph Gaussian processes to be more easily integrated within deep learning architectures, such as neural networks, compared to their current form. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation and city management systems and is critical for providing a smooth journey experience to citizens and a robust, efficient transportation service to city visitors. Current methods for monitoring urban road conditions are costly and typically limited to collecting data from a few strategic locations, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of the condition of the entire urban road network. In this study, we assess the potential of ridesharing services as a cost-effective means of gathering data on the condition of urban roads at a massive scale. We develop a travel cost model that takes into consideration various factors such as the condition of roads, pricing policies, and the routing behavior of ridesharing passengers, and use it to determine the optimal locations for collecting data on the condition of urban roads. We also conduct a thorough analysis of the characteristics of the road network and the impact of ridesharing on it, and investigate how different pricing policies influence the decision-making process of riders in optimal sensing strategies. This research involves the use of simulation and real-world data from Didi Chuxing in Beijing and Shanghai. The findings show that road conditions significantly affect the routing behavior of ridesharing passengers, especially on longer journeys, and that the location of sensing bases can be determined cost-effectively by reducing the impact of road conditions on passenger routing. This also leads to a significant reduction in the cost of discovering the condition of urban roads. The research concludes with an analysis of the limitations of the study and potential areas for further research on this topic. The issue of discovering the condition of urban roads is becoming increasingly more important, and more research is needed to explore alternative methods of data collection, such as the use of motorcycle couriers, bicycle couriers and electric bike-sharing services. The problem of finding the minimum number of locations to visit in order to discover the condition of urban roads is also an important issue, and more research is needed to solve this problem, especially in large-scale networks. The article is to be presented at the 2019 IEEE Intelligent Transportation Systems Conference. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Additionally, our research demonstrated that J/ψ invisible decays into photon and neutrino or dark matter offer complementary and independent sensitivity to these fundamental phenomena, providing valuable insights that can be gained through studies of hadron physics. In the process, we established that the likelihood fit method is an efficient and precise approach for implications analysis. Lastly, our research highlighted the implication of J/ψ invisible decays for dark photon theories, demonstrating that the most stringent limits on this theory's mass scale are already within the reach of existing J/ψ data, with a study of purely invisible decays capable of further improving these bounds by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, our study revealed that hadron experiments can contribute significantly to dark matter detection, with even light dark matter mass ranges amenable to direct detection already constrained by J/ψ decay into invisible matter. As such, our research recommends that in addition to searching for visible photons, experiments like the Belle II also consider analyzing data for light dark matter and dark photons. This additional analysis of purely invisible photon spectra will provide even more stringent limits on light dark matter and dark photon mass scales, effectively increasing the sensitivity of hadron experiments to these fundamental phenomena by at least one order of magnitude. Consequently, our research demonstrates that hadron experiments, in particular J/ψ decay into invisible matter, offer the most compelling implications for light dark matter detection,

We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Compared to existing methods, our new variable stepsize SGLMs require significantly fewer evaluations of the given function, and we take advantage of this efficiency in solving a real-world population dynamics model. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examine the underlying features that influence the automated scoring models developed with deep learning techniques. We utilize both qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze various aspects of the models' behavior, including their reliance on biased data, their tendency to overfit, and their failure to capture essay quality dimensions. The models' tendency to place excessive importance on irrelevant information and their difficulty in being distinguished from similar models were also examined. The findings indicate that the models exhibit both over-sensitivity and over-stability, which hinders their effectiveness. We propose several strategies for enhancing the robustness and performance of automated scoring models, including the integration of essay-specific pre-training methods, adversarial training, and unbiased evaluation protocols. Our research provides both theoretical and practical contributions to the field of automated assessment. By improving the reliability and validity of deep learning-based automated scoring models, we can have confidence in their ability to support the decision-making processes used in education and other applications. The techniques presented in this paper can also be applied to other high-stakes applications involving the evaluation of complex written materials. The case studies and model implementations described in this paper can serve as reference examples for the development and evaluation of deep learning-based automated scoring models in various contexts. The findings and methodologies presented in this research can inform the development of future high-performance models that are both robust and effective. The techniques discussed in this paper can be adapted for application to other complex tasks involving the evaluation of written content. The research described in this paper demonstrates the value of subject expertise in the development and evaluation of deep learning-based models for complex, real-world applications. The methods and metrics used in this paper can be applied to other similar problems in the field of artificial intelligence and machine learning. The findings of this research can be applied to other automated scoring systems used in education and other fields. The data preprocessing techniques presented in this paper can be adapted for application to other natural language processing tasks. The paper raises important concerns about the reliability and validity of deep learning-based automated scoring models and highlights the need for further research into their development and evaluation. The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk. It follows that $\phi(0,b) = 1/3$ and $\phi(1,b) = 1/6$ with an intensive persistence front $f(x) = \lim_{t\to\infty} t^{-1}\phi(x,t)/2$ exhibiting an abrupt change from $f(0)=1/3-1/6=1/2$ to $f(1)=1/6$ as $x$ increases through the origin. The result relies on recent findings regarding the random walk's local time statistics. Additionally, an alternative approach to studying persistence is proposed with discussion on further implications and potential extensions to other stochastic processes. Furthermore, the proposed framework is utilized to identify an unsolved conjecture related to the standard two-sided random walk. The proposed method is a systematic expansion of the probability distribution of the random walk's local time, enabling the derivation of persistence probabilities via the inverse of the proposed density function's derivative. This strategy is a more general and versatile approach than previous methods, such as the 'dream' formula, and is applicable to various extensions and variations of the random walk. The results obtained through this method are verified through numerical simulations, ensuring the accuracy of the theoretical predictions. The theoretical approach is a powerful tool for analyzing and understanding the persistence properties of random walks, while numerical simulations serve as a means of validating the results and the proposed model's effectiveness. The results presented are applicable across a broad spectrum of random walk scenarios, encompassing various definitions and modifications of the standard random walk. The persistence of random walks is a fundamental area of study

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. Properties of the plasma in this mode were found to be suitable for accurate, coherent interrogation of plasma by radio frequency fields. Furthermore, the requirements for a plasma source similar to IShTAR's to support the ELM-sympathetic disruption research are discussed. It is determined that a plasma source with a length of at least 0.3 meters is necessary to maintain the required density across a wide range of conditions. Additionally, the limitations of the test facility IShTAR in replicating disruption conditions are highlighted, and future potential improvements to the plasma source are also identified. The results of this study demonstrate the capability of the IShTAR plasma source to support research into disruption phenomena. Furthermore, the findings may be of value to researchers working on the development of plasma sources for large-scale fusion experiments due to the similarities in design and requirements. Building on this knowledge, the IShTAR team is considering the implementation of a gas injection system that utilizes microholes, which have been effectively utilized in the ISTOK facility in Russia. However, any such modification would need to address several technical issues and potential risks before its safety could be verified. In the meantime, the researchers are proposing an alternative gas injection system with ring-shaped holes, which could also provide the necessary particle flux required for a plasma state without the complexities of microholes. This alternative solution could potentially be safer and more practical for implementation on existing facilities like IShTAR. Furthermore, upgrading the plasma diagnosis capabilities, particularly the electron temperature measurement method, could further enhance the knowledge gained from operating the IShTAR test facility. Lastly, the findings from this study may also be of value to researchers working on the development of plasma sources for large-scale fusion

This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies. A global periodic solution for the system's ODE is provided, along with the direction and speed of bifurcation periodic solution changes. This research offers insights into designing nematode formulations that promote sustainable pest control. This modified model exhibits more complex dynamics, including the possibility of nematode population decline, but still reaches a globally stable equilibrium or periodic solution. The model's parameters are derived from the Norgay model, which is a system of two nonlinear differential equations representing the population dynamics of two species in an ecological environment. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort and resources. Automatic image analysis can complement and enhance the process by reducing costs and the burden on pathologists. However, developing accurate and robust methods for detecting cancer cells within tissue samples is complex due to the diverse range of sample preparations and visual characteristics. In this study, a new nucleus region detection approach, W-Net, is introduced, focusing on colon cancer cell detection within H&E stained tissue samples. W-Net leverages a two-stage framework, first using a local patch-based network to pinpoint potential nucleus regions and then utilizing a global network to refine the detections while ensuring nucleus format. Evaluations using 1000 randomly selected patches yielded a notable 57.46% mAP improvement for nucleus region detection over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, experiments demonstrating cancer vs. non-cancer cell classification, along with a combined score with nucleus detection, led to a 73.17% overall accuracy rate. All code and models are openly available for use and adaptation. In addition to presenting the new detection approach, a comprehensive overview of existing techniques for nucleus and cell segmentation in histopathology is also provided. Furthermore, key evaluation metrics along with practical implementation details for cancer vs. non-cancer cell classification are also discussed. Finally, future research directions for cancer diagnosis using W-Net are also presented. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. This knowledge can be used to make more informed decisions regarding the utilization of anti-inflammatory drugs in treating COVID-19. This research is an effort to highlight the value of single-cell modeling within the broader context of the host-dynamics of COVID-19, and biologically-based computational modeling, in general, but also highlights the limited access to single-cell data, a common challenge, at least with respect to the specific data utilized in this study. This research is continuing to monitor the host-dynamics of COVID-19 beyond pyroptosis, with cell death due to apoptosis, and is expanding to other types of cell death, as well as other types of inflammation, in an effort to more comprehensively understand the complex interplay of host-cell dynamics that are being affected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. This work is also being used to validate the use of rodent models due to their widespread use in life sciences research, with a special emphasis on research centered on host-dynamics of COVID-19, by demonstrating the similarity between the expression levels of key genes in both human and rodent models, as well as the response to treatment, as predicted by the single-cell model, as evidence of the model's predictive accuracy, as well as the use of machine learning, with an emphasis on Random Forest, due to its widespread use

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. The development of HELMHOLTZ is showcased through the successful verification of over 150 test cases for a Michelson library containing over 300 pre-defined functions. Additionally, guidelines are provided for users to implement their own refinements with Michelson's user-defined functions and datatypes. The design of a Michelson proof manager is also described, enabling the recursive refinement of programs, and a method for the abstraction of program properties, leading to the achievement of a 'proof-of-concept' for the verification of compound transactions. Furthermore, the performance of HELMHOLTZ is evaluated and compared to other verification tools. Lastly, future directions for both HELMHOLTZ and refinement types in the Tezos ecosystem are discussed. With its innovative use of refinement types and a proof manager, HELMHOLTZ is positioned to contribute significantly to the advancement of the Tezos compiler and the development of safe and reliable smart contracts. As the first static verification tool for the Tezos compiler, HELMHOLTZ is designed to be an open-source and modular verification tool that can be utilized by developers in the creation of secure and dependable smart contracts. The development of this project is part of the PhD research in Computer Science at the University of Cambridge, supervised by Klaus Ostermann and Jérémie Horel, with additional guidance from Anthea Powell. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Finally, the unique properties of GCNNs are then highlighted by comparing and contrasting them with both standard CNNs and Fully Connected Neural Networks, Additionally, the unique ability of GCNNs to effectively learn from node coordinates and graph topology is also highlighted, followed by a discussion on future research possibilities and potential applications of GCNNs in the analysis of complex datasets across various fields. We anticipate this intuitive explanation of GCNNs to be of use to both experienced practitioners and new students of Neural Network architecture, seeking to provide a clear and comprehensive exploration of GCNNs from initial implementation to potential areas of application. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Formerly, all coreset algorithms for $k$-means in Euclidean space required exponential storage in relation to $d$. We also present an extension to a distributed setting and a novel one-pass $k$-forest algorithm for minimizing the sum of distances to nodes in a metric tree. These innovations build upon our discovery that a significant subset of past $k$-means points can be stored as representatives with the property that the cumulative storage forms a coreset for the $k$-means problem. We demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms through an experimental analysis involving synthetic and real-world datasets. Through further analysis and experimentation of a proposed boosting scheme, we find that it yields improved clustering results in comparison to standard $k$-means and accelerates algorithm execution while maintaining approximate solution quality. Finally, we investigate the algorithmic properties that guarantee strong solution guarantees and propose directions for optimizing further the algorithm's performance. The algorithm we introduce achieves better practical performance compared to optimized baseline methods for large-scale datasets in medium to high-dimensional spaces. The code for the proposed algorithms is available at https://github.com/AmirArceli/dynamic-clusiters. Through our work, we address fundamental challenges and explore innovative solutions for dynamic high-dimensional clustering problems, revealing new perspectives on coreset construction and the potential for future breakthroughs. The study of dynamic data streams and coreset algorithms can lead to significant insights and advancements in various fields, such as machine learning, signal processing, and database management. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits the decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Furthermore, we find that even basic heuristic approaches can yield reasonable outcomes under certain conditions, highlighting the potential of the hierarchical framework to be adaptable and overcame by various issues in grid world representations. Our research provides a valuable framework for analyzing the interplay between large scale and finer detailed representations in the context of stochastic game playing. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. 

Building on the concepts of 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' probabilities, we explore related 'polyhedral' probabilities. To do this, we first need to define a particular type of polyhedron, referred to as a 'cyclic polyhedron'. Then, we establish the probability of a random 'cyclic polyhedron' having the property of being convex, and examine the limitations and implications of this concept in various dimensions. 

Our study of these ideas also leads to a new proof for a well-known theorem regarding the probability of a random convex polyhedron. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be implemented with just 9 million parameters compared to 18 million for the traditional cycleGAN method. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms the conventional cycleGAN approach in terms of quantitative evaluation and visual quality. Furthermore, experiments conducted on a CT-specific dataset hold promising implications for applying the AdaIN-Switchable cycleGAN (ASCAN) method to other medical image transformations. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes. Furthermore, alarm bells are sounded for potential issues related to dialog understanding, data contamination, and labeled data's side effects in the accompanying technical report. Additionally, proposals including future research directions, new data sets, and guidelines for dialog understanding in-the-wild are also included. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. When applying these samples to estimate the mean of the posterior, our results showed improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in the PSNR metric. We also found that optimizing a conditional GAN with an entropic regularization led to more stable and efficient training by preventing mode collapse and reducing sensitivity to hyperparameter choices. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This particular screen, dubbed the 'Upper Crust' screen, is distinguished by its unique combination of proximity, angular radius, and orientation. The screens' properties may provide insight into the structure and composition of the local interstellar medium. Furthermore, the upper boundary of the Local Bubble's extent above the plane of the Sun has been estimated at approximately 18.72 arcseconds in radius angle, and further research into the Upper Crust screen may shed light on the characteristics of the local upper boundary layer of the Local Bubble. The findings from this study may also contribute to a greater understanding of how the local interstellar medium is affected by the Sun's presence, potentially providing insight into how the Sun's movement within the galaxy may impact the surrounding environment. Additionally, this research may lead to a greater understanding of how the local bistable structure, composed of the Local Bubble and the Upper Crust screen, forms and evolves over time. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Moreover, within the realm of stable categories, shadows are shown to be directly computable via the bicategorical trace functor, extending a preceding corollary regarding stable homotopy theory. The theory of shadows is then applied to provide a more intricate interpretation of the bicategorical Thom space construction. Ultimately, this leads to an identification of the THH of the sphere bicategory with a simplified form, encompassing a combined analysis of both its geometric and algebraic components. This result, in turn, gives rise to novel proofs for several aspects of the bicategorical McKinnon's theorem. The d\'ecalage functors are themselves found to preserve Morita equivalence and serve as a key means of computing the THH of a bicategory. Furthermore, this is further illustrated through the computation of THH for several categories of algebraic structures, including categories of Lie algebras, Poisson algebras, and algebras with a braiding. The theory of shadows is then used to prove a statement regarding the relationship between the THH of a bicategory and the THH of its subfactor, itself an instance of a more general bicategorical version of the principle of compositionality. This principle can be seen as a formal expression of the idea that the THH of a bicategory should be determined by the THH of its full subcategories of objects that are mutually isomorphic in a specific way. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video rather than web images. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. To enhance the difficulty of sound source localization tasks, we introduce a technique called hard positive sampling that identifies challenging image elements and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. This approach, though seemingly counterproductive, proves effective in several datasets and scenarios. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the difficulty of certain image elements and the performance of sound source localization. Our research indicates that easily identified elements can hinder the learning process and result in inferior performance. Moreover, we discover that certain easy elements can mask the difficulty of other elements, making it difficult to determine the overall difficulty of an image. Lastly, we explore the application of our technique to other vision-and-sound fusion tasks, including sound-related image retrieval and video auditing. Our method outperforms the competitors on the Flickr SoundNet dataset but lags behind state-of-the-art methods on the VGG-Sound Source dataset. It is worth noting that although our algorithm performs well on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, it does not fully leverage the available annotation information, specifically the sound source labels, which only serve as a binary indication of whether the object generating the sound is present in the image. In contrast, the VGG-Sound Source dataset features precise bounding box annotations that define the location of the sound source within the image. Our algorithm fails to fully exploit this additional information, which, as demonstrated by the results, results in subpar performance. It is our intention to investigate other methods that make use of this detailed annotation information to further improve sound source localization performance. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The implemented open-source code is available on https://github.com/DingHuaXiao/LGCN. Furthermore, an accompanying study published on arXiv 2021 can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00003. The model's papers and code have been highly influential in the field of graph convolutional networks under hyperbolic geometry. The code has been republished at https://github.com/ChangHeLi/LCN-Code, and the model's recent extensions with multi-layer LGCN have been made available at https://github.com/ChangHeLi/LGCN-Code/tree/master/ML-LGCN. The model's recent extensions with multi-layer LGCN have outperformed all existing methods on 3 classification tasks and 2 link prediction tasks, as shown in the accompanying updated code at https://github.com/ChangHeLi/LGCN-Code/tree/master/ML-LGCN. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Notably, the source term's decay rate in the L^2 norm is found to be (t+1)^{-1/2}, which is the same rate as the solution of the direct problem. A numerical strategy based on the boundary control method has been proposed and successfully applied to a simplified model. This involves modifying the equation to make the source term accessible from the boundary, then using the boundary control method to recover the original source term. This numerical strategy demonstrates the possibility of recovering the source term via the boundary control method, but further work is needed to tackle the original inverse problem directly. Overall, this research highlights the complexity and challenges associated with the non-compact boundary source inverse problem. Finally, potential future directions for this project are discussed. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this report seeks to address various misconceptions regarding negative temperature that have been presented in various educational modules. It is intended for use in an advanced undergraduate or early graduate-level physics course. Some key points from the report can be found in the appendix. It is essential for students to have a background in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics before studying negative absolute temperature. It is also important to note that while negative absolute temperature can be understood through classical means, it is primarily a phenomenon of quantum systems. It is not a feature of classical thermodynamics. It is not a temperature at which systems can exist for extended periods. It is an imperative transient state that can only be achieved by non-equilibrium methods and is not demonstrated through conventional means such as the curve crossing in a van der Waals diagram. It is also not a standard temperature for any molecular or atomic system. It is a critical concept, however, in the study of the Lamb shift and the stabilization of states in quantum systems. It is not a temperature that can be perceived through the emission or absorption of light as it does not indicate a shift in the emission or absorption spectra. It is not a universal feature of all quantum systems as it depends on the specific conditions of these systems. It is not a feature of multi-level systems as it is primarily a phenomenon of two-level systems. It is not a feature of systems in steady-state as it only appears in the transient state. It is not a feature of open systems as it only appears in closed systems. It is not a feature of classical systems as it is a quantum phenomenon. It is not a feature of systems that can lose energy as it only appears in systems that cannot lose energy. It is not a feature of systems that can be cooled to the ground state as it only appears in systems that cannot be cooled to the ground state. It is not a feature of systems that can be heated to the point of destruction as it only appears in systems that cannot be heated to the point of destruction. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. UniToPatho is unique in its comprehensive scope, covering a wide range of topics including non-neoplastic findings, benign and malignant neoplasms, and adenomas classified as low, medium, and high risk; it also features diverse subtypes of neoplastic patterns. To facilitate easy access to these annotations, we've developed a Label Collector Application (LCA) that enables multiple experts to collaboratively annotate whole-slide images. By utilizing a combination of specialized software and open-source tools for image processing, we've generated a set of high-quality, down-sampled patches that can be used for deep learning-based approaches while also extracting valuable information for subsequent exploration of the data. These annotations include neoplastic/non-neoplastic classifications, as well as grades for adenomas (low, medium, and high risk); they also encode information about the location of specific patterns within each image. To facilitate further advancements in the field, we're releasing UniToPatho as an open-source dataset available under the UniToPatho License, a custom variation of the BSD 3-Clause License. We've also introduced a challenge related to the dataset, where participants can submit their models for evaluation and comparison to established benchmarks. The leaderboard for this challenge can be found on the competition website associated with this dataset. We believe that ongoing research projects, like the one described in this paper, have the potential to significantly contribute to the development of innovative solutions for the characterization of colorectal polyps. UniToPatho is a labeled histopathological dataset designed for the classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas based on H&E stained tissue samples. Created by the Department of Biopathology at UniTo, this dataset has been made available to the research community and will be used in an associated challenge.

The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of the solution of an acoustic wave problem on a domain $D$ with a plane wave propagating in the exterior domain $D_\epsilon$, along with an interface condition on the boundary $\Gamma_\epsilon$. The proposed scheme involves dividing the domain into elements and employing an alternative form of the reduced dimensionality format, specifically the edge-based Nodal Discontinuous Galerkin (NDG) method. This approach minimizes the number of degrees of freedom required compared to traditional finite element methods. It also introduces an optimal adaptive refinement strategy in two dimensions, based on an edge-based marker-and-kill technique. This results in significantly improved solutions with a much lower number of degrees of freedom than would be required with a fixed mesh size. Extensive numerical tests have been conducted to demonstrate the method's reliability, both with and without the adaptive technique. For the adaptive cases, the method was able to produce accurate results at a much lower cost than the non-adaptive method, potentially making it suitable for more complex problems involving the scattering of high-frequency waves. However, further research is needed to fully explore the method's potential for such problems. The proposed method may also be applicable to other types of wave equations, such as the elastic wave equations, but this requires further investigation. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. However, further research is needed to fully understand the implications of these discoveries. As such, the existing model for the development of the inner Solar System remains applicable, and there is still a need for water delivered to the planets through late-stage active accretion processes.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains. Furthermore, we demonstrate affine quantum-group symmetry properties, such as the coproduct, antipode, and Yang-Baxter equation, being preserved by the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's inverse and evolution operators. These preserved properties ensure the correct transmission of quantum-group symmetry to physical observables, guaranteeing their self-consistency. This work offers a significant insight into the affine quantum-group symmetry of interacting one-dimensional systems. Additionally, we illustrate how to apply the quantum-group symmetry to correlate particles separated by arbitrary distances within spin chains of various spin multiplicities. Finally, our findings provide a crucial proof for the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's validity as an exact solver for spin chains possessing affine quantum-group symmetry. This approval covers a vast class of integrable models, including the isotropic and anisotropic XX, XXZ, YY, YYZ, ZZ, ZZZZ, and XYZ chains, all of which possess $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$ symmetry. This approval extends even further to their multi-chain generalizations, guaranteeing the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's precise accuracy. This approval comes with the additional condition that the anisotropy parameter $\Delta$ must lie within the range $[-1, 1]$. This range ensures the uniqueness of the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's eigenvalue solutions, alongside the correctness of the obtained form factors and correlation functions. This approval now enables a thorough examination of physical properties throughout these interacting quantum systems. This knowledge will be vital for exploring the effects of quantum integrability present within these discrete, unified systems. This understanding will be crucial as these systems transition into the continuous limit required to model real-world phenomena. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Our models also hold advantage over the existing state-of-the-art models in multiple zero-shot language pairs. The code for our work is available at https://github.com/parag-ks/zero-shot-s2t. Word embeddings used in our work can be found at https://github.com/parag-ks/zero-shot-s2t/tree/main/utils/word-embeddings. GShuff: A Simple yet Effective Sentence-backdoor Attack Method for Integrating Adversarial Samples into Real-world Data for Enhancing Model Robustness can be found at https://github.com/zhkloong/press-release-write-up. The paper zero-shot speech-to-text translation was not formally published but is based on papers titled: Zero-shot Speech-to-text Translation via Joint Speech-to-Text Learning at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.09064 and Multi-Sample-Sentence-Backdoor-Attack-and-Offer at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07999. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. A simple harmonic oscillator model explains the relationship between multipoles and their responses to incident light. We also examine the angular dependence of optical force and scattering behavior. Furthermore, we investigate how the choice of material affects optical force and scattering patterns. A new method is introduced for calculating the multipoles of arbitrary particles cross-sectional shapes, building upon the success of our previous approach devised by Serracino et al. and extensively tested for various particles across the dipolar to Mie regimes. This new method is capable of handling particles with complex internal structures, dielectric cavities, and non-spherical particles, such as dumbells and elliptical disks. The accuracy of these multipoles is validated by a thorough comparison with conventional calculations using Mie theory and extends the applicability of our previous approach to smaller wavelengths appropriate for semiconductor particles. This new approach also facilitates an insightful harmonic oscillator analysis of our findings. A key advantage of our multipoles is their capacity to model the angular dependence of optical force and scattering behavior, revealing an irregular dependence that diverges from the typical dipolar behavior. This is particularly significant for particles larger than a few micrometers, where backscattering may substantially deviate from forward scattering. This fundamental understanding of optical force and scattering patterns is anticipated to provide the groundwork for novel applications and enhanced performance in field-driven particle manipulation, optical nonreciprocity, and optomechanics. A new theoretical model is proposed to describe the optomechanical response of particles in vacuum, building upon our multipoles and harmonically analyzed interatomic forces. This model is demonstrated with examples of silicon and carbon atoms across multiple regimes, from the Mie to the dipolar limit, and includes a detailed analysis of its components, including the contribution of each multipole and force type across different wavelengths. This model enables a deeper understanding of the optomechanical properties of atoms and molecules, shedding light on the fundamental relationship between the structure of matter and its response to light,

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues. Further, algebraic limit passage towards U(gl(n)) is attainable through Olshanski decomposition and filtered algebra direct and inverse limits. Ultimately, this framework enables expansion of representations to infinite-dimensional Schur modules. Lastly, an observation regarding algebra U(o(n)) is included. This research is a follow-up to our prior work entitled "Quantum immanants and the Harish-Chandra isomorphism" also available at arXiv:1812.06213. That initial study proposed the quantum immanants hypothesis in the context of U(gl(n)), which has since been proven by Brubaker, Mason and Petersen in their paper "An proof of the quantum immanants conjecture for U(gl(n))" arXiv:1912.04416, a result on which we expand here. This study on U(gl(n)) has implications for U(o(n)), as we demonstrate analogous results there, with due consideration of the differences between the algebras. This research is a follow-up to our prior work mentioned above and we are grateful to the referees for their suggestions and the excellent peer review they provided. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. Moreover, we validate our approach by applying it to well-studied Ru and Os oxides, where it accurately reproduces available data, while also identifying potential for $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing to be crucial in other 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. The results from this study can be utilized in further research to pinpoint the relative contributions of spin-orbit coupling, electron-electron interactions, and crystal field splitting in these complex materials. Additionally, we suggest that in some cases, depending on the specific details of each material, its unique phase diagram might be attributed to $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the significance of considering $d$-orbital mixing in any attempt to develop a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic and crystalline electronic structures in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. The knowledge gained from these calculations can be employed to reinterpret and reconcile the outcomes from various experimental and theoretical studies in these materials. Moreover, this knowledge can be used to identify potential $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in other 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, where this effect is shown to be a common phenomenon. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Despite the promising results, there are restrictions on applying these techniques in clinical settings due to the need for a trained expert to operate the system and the limited robustness of the model in detecting a broad spectrum of conditions. In addition, further research is needed to examine the scientific validity of this approach. We have made our model publicly available for third-party testing and evaluation. We plan on expanding our research to handle the segmentation of multiple medical conditions from chest X-rays. Additionally, we will investigate more sophisticated techniques for the manipulation of medical conditions and the creation of realistic medical images. Furthermore, we will conduct a patient-based evaluation to assess the safety and reliability of this approach. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. In one experiment, we modify the numerical experiment from Kalashnikov and Klein to solve a boundary value problem for the Laplace equation on a grid consisting of an L-shaped region. Our results show that using our high-order method with a small grid yields more accurate solutions than the methods based on Kalashnikov and Klein's results. We also explore how our method can be applied to a non-smooth function by using a small modification and a substantial decrease in costs for computations. In addition, we discuss the connections of our high-order method to other high-order methods and we make publicly available the Python code used in our experiments. Furthermore, we discuss and provide evidence that our method based on high-order approximations for near field computations is more than one order of magnitude faster than the Nystrom method based on low-order approximations for a wide range of grid sizes. In fact, when using a small grid of $128 \times 128$ cells, our method is almost two orders of magnitude faster than the Nystrom method. In contrast to grid-based methods, our new method offers comparable performance for a significantly smaller computational cost.
